d83c2801a: main.js runs before the DOM as a render-blocking script, so getElementById returns null; swup transitions also caused the global click handler to be bound repeatedly, finally bailed out with a window._fireworkBound flag

All of these are things a component lifecycle gives you for free; hand-rolling means hitting them one by one.
One more thing that’s easy to forget: URLs have to be preserved exactly… Hexo’s abbrlink short link (crc16/dec, permalink is p/:abbrlink/) became a Hugo slug, then became work.id on the new site — /p/{id}/ survived three generations of that old link. Not even the trailing slash can change — Artalk/Valine historical comments are stored under the path /p/{id}/ with the slash, and missing one character means losing comments. To that end, vns-next had to disable the framework’s built-in trailing-slash redirect and take over itself; I posted the full comments from that tug-of-war in the post about convention files.
Finally, one intermediate state. The bbps site is also output: 'export', with next.config.ts only 12 lines, and real-time data simply bypassed with client-side polling:
useEffect(() => {
  fetchStats()
  const id = setInterval(fetchStats, 30000)
  return () => clearInterval(id)
}, [fetchStats])
Hit an external API every 30 seconds — good enough… Static shell + client polling, effortless.
A month of moving things around, and it really boiled down to one question: is there anything on this site that absolutely has to live on a server? Think it over and the answer is obvious—there’s no mystery to it. Anyway, I’m out~

title: My CLAUDE.md Is Only One Line: How Much Should a Convention File Actually Contain
content:
I recently rewrote a Galgame resource site entirely from Hugo to Next.js. The repo is vns-next. From the initial commit create-next-app to being deployable, it took 13 commits over less than 20 hours.
When I looked back through the repo afterward, I noticed something pretty funny — the convention file I wrote for Claude is just one line long. And I didn’t even write that line myself…
This post isn’t about rendering modes or deployment. It’s only about one thing: “what conventions should you leave for AI when starting a project.” Let me record the conclusions I’ve worked out after bouncing between several projects…
 My entire CLAUDE.md is one line
Here’s the original — the full contents of CLAUDE.md in the root of vns-next:
@AGENTS.md
Yep, that’s the whole thing, using import syntax to point at the neighboring AGENTS.md. Now let’s look at AGENTS.md@ — all 5 lines:
<!-- BEGIN:nextjs-agent-rules -->
# This is NOT the Next.js you know

This version has breaking changes — APIs, conventions, and file structure may all differ from your training data. Read the relevant guide in `node_modules/next/dist/docs/` before writing any code. Heed deprecation notices.
<!-- END:nextjs-agent-rules -->
Notice that pair of BEGIN / END markers — I didn’t write that part; create-next-app inserted it itself. The core message is just one sentence: don’t trust the Next.js in your training data, go read node_modules/next/dist/docs/ before writing any code.
When I started thdl (a Touhou doujin resource site) earlier, it was the same setup — CLAUDE.md was identical, also a one-line import pointing to AGENTS.md, same contents word for word. The benefit is obvious: a single source of truth, so the two rule sets can’t conflict with each other~
So is that little enough? Is it enough to get by? At first I definitely thought it wasn’t enough…
 The other extreme: one repo, three sets of convention files
That earlier project acg-site took the completely opposite approach — maintaining three sets at once:

CLAUDE.md in the root, 111 lines
9 .mdc files under .cursor/rules/, among which project.mdc and library-versions.mdc are alwaysApply: true
.github/copilot-instructions.md, which demotes itself to an index right at the top: "For the complete conventions, see the project root CLAUDE.md"

Line 3 of CLAUDE.md opens like this:

Freshness warning: This project uses a large number of cutting-edge library versions that AI training data very likely doesn’t cover. When you hit an uncertain API usage, be sure to check the latest docs (Context7 MCP is available in Cursor).

Then it dedicates a whole section to “Key version differences (common AI mistakes),” 6 items:
- `params` / `searchParams` 在 Next.js 16 中是 **Promise**，服务端用 `await`，客户端用 `use()`
- Tailwind v4 用 **CSS 配置**（`@import "tailwindcss"` + `@theme {}`），无 `tailwind.config.ts`
- Prisma 7 generator 为 `"prisma-client"`（不是 `"prisma-client-js"`），导入路径 `@/generated/prisma/client`
- Zod 4 导入 `import { z } from "zod"`（不是 `zod/v4`）
- 日期用 `dayjs`，不用 `date-fns`
- 认证用 Better Auth（`@/lib/auth-client`），不是 next-auth
At the end of .cursor/rules/library-versions.mdc there’s also a ❌→✅ comparison table, 7 rows:
1. ❌ `params.id` → ✅ `(await params).id` 或 `use(params).id`
2. ❌ `tailwind.config.ts` 的 `theme.extend` → ✅ `globals.css` 的 `@theme { }`
3. ❌ `import { PrismaClient } from "@prisma/client"` → ✅ `import { PrismaClient } from "@/generated/prisma/client"`
4. ❌ `provider = "prisma-client-js"` → ✅ `provider = "prisma-client"`
5. ❌ `import { z } from "zod/v4"` → ✅ `import { z } from "zod"`
6. ❌ 用 `date-fns` 处理日期 → ✅ 用 `dayjs`
7. ❌ 用 `next-auth` API → ✅ 用 Better Auth（`@/lib/auth-client`）
This one is genuinely useful. Because everything it writes is stuff AI can’t possibly know — version differences. The generator name in Prisma 7 changed, the import path in Zod 4 changed — if that isn’t written down, the model will whip you up a version based on the old way it remembers, and then you’ll spend twenty minutes debugging an import that doesn’t even exist. I’ve paid that bill several times…
 The cost of three sets of files is drift
In the commit 519e5a7 I updated the docs and split apart a wrong explanation in CLAUDE.md — the original said "pnpm lint — ESLint + TypeScript check," but in package.json, lint only runs eslint . and doesn’t include type checking at all. After the fix it’s three items:
- `pnpm lint` — 仅 ESLint
- `pnpm typecheck` — 仅 TypeScript 类型检查（`tsc --noEmit`）
- `pnpm check` — ESLint + TypeScript 类型检查（提交前完整校验）
The same commit also filled in the version numbers: tRPC 11.15 → 11.17, Zod 4.3 → 4.4, Prisma 7.6 → 7.8, Better Auth 1.5 → 1.6.
And then? .cursor/rules/project.mdc still says tRPC 11.15, Zod 4.3, Prisma 7.6, Better Auth 1.5 to this day, and even that wrong lint explanation is still lying there as-is. I updated one and forgot the other — that’s exactly how drift happens…
In a repo with multiple collaborators this gets even worse: two AI tools each read their own directory and end up with contexts that aren’t even the same document. I wrote about that scenario separately in another post, so I won’t expand on it here.
Convention files are code too — they expire. And no CI will tell you they’ve expired…
 So where does the knowledge actually live
Looking back at vns-next: no .claude/, no .cursor/, no .github/, no docs/, no task list and no spec doc. Yet it’s not short on context at all.
Because all the knowledge is written into code comments and commit bodies~
In next.config.ts, that stretch of trailingSlash nails down both “why” and “why we also have to turn off the built-in one”:
// 与旧站（Hugo）URL 完全一致：尾斜杠必须保留，
// Artalk/Valine 历史评论按 /p/{id}/ 路径存储，去掉斜杠会丢评论
trailingSlash: true,
// 但内置的尾斜杠 308 会把 POST /api/auth/* 重定向成 /api/auth/*/ 导致 404（Better Auth 全挂），
// 故关掉内置重定向，由 src/proxy.ts 只对页面 GET 请求补尾斜杠
skipTrailingSlashRedirect: true,
src/proxy.ts:21-23 is a pure warning, written for the next person who wants to “optimize” this code (most likely AI):
// 注意：不能用 nextUrl.clone() 再改 pathname——NextURL 的 setter 会按
// trailingSlash 配置把尾斜杠再规范化掉，Location 指回自身造成死循环。
// 官方 skipTrailingSlashRedirect 示例即用裸 new URL() 构造。
src/lib/cache.ts:1-5 spells out how this file will be replaced in the future:
/**
 * 内存 TTL 缓存 helper
 *
 * 接口对齐 acgn-flow 的 redis helper（getCache/setCache/deleteCache/deleteCachePattern），
 * 将来若要换 ioredis 可以无痛替换本文件实现，调用方不需要改动。
 */
The message of commit b07e20d even writes down the verification method — I went into the pitfall itself (no database at build time) in another post, so here I’ll just look at what it stuffed into the commit body:
fix(deploy): 全站 force-dynamic——Docker 构建环境无数据库，静态预渲染必然失败

根 layout 声明 dynamic='force-dynamic'（查库页面请求时渲染，内存缓存兜底），
sitemap/feed.xml/llms.txt/index.xml 同步声明。已用死库 DATABASE_URL 本地复现
构建通过。
(This is part 1 of 2 of the same post.)
What these places have in common is that they will definitely be read next time. Anyone modifying proxy.ts will inevitably see that infinite-loop warning, and anyone reading next.config.ts will inevitably see where the trailing slash came from. Whether docs/architecture.md ever gets opened, though, is pure luck…
 How I split it up now



Content type
Where it goes
Frequency of use




Framework version differences and API pitfalls
CLAUDE.md
★★★★★


Why a particular line of code is written that way
Code comments
★★★★★


The motivation and verification method for a change
commit body
★★★★


Deployment and ops steps
A separate README
★★★


Project intro, directory structure
Don’t write it, it’ll go stale
★



Only the first category is something the model could never infer from the code — if you don’t write it down, it simply doesn’t know. As for things like “this project uses the App Router, and the directory structure is as follows…”, the model gets that with a quick ls~
 While I’m at it, some self-deprecation about the README
Speaking of things that go stale. The README of vns-next is still the default create-next-app template to this day — 36 lines, talking about npm/yarn/pnpm/bun run dev and Deploy on Vercel, not a single character changed since the initial commit 85aa812.
But this project is actually self-hosted with bun + Docker Compose, and deployment never went through Vercel at all (that VERCEL branch in next.config.ts is just a fallback). The README and reality are completely out of sync…
Still, .dockerignore:13-19 says this:
# 内容导出快照 / 文档 / 部署自身
content-export
deploy
README.md
AGENTS.md
CLAUDE.md
.claude
README, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, and .claude are all excluded from the image context together (.claude is just a precaution — this project never actually created that directory). So I simply couldn’t be bothered to change it — it can’t make it into the image anyway…
Incidentally, 12 of those 13 commits carry the Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 trailer; the only one without it is the initial commit generated by create-next-app. The author on every commit is me — credit where credit is due, but the blame is mine too~
Anyway, my next project will probably still be just one line, and I’ll add to it once I hit a snag~

title: 9 Commits, Not a Single Human Author: After an AI Wrote an Entire Project Alone
content:
Recently I took over a project someone dumped on me. I pulled it down with git log and paused for a second — 9 commits, all authored by the same AI Dev <ai-dev@local>, not a single human commit. I won’t paste hashes for the commits I mention below; I’ll just refer to them by what they did. The repo has no CLAUDE.md, no AGENTS.md, no .claude/, no .cursor/, no CI, lint is just tsc --noEmit, and tests are nonexistent. I spent a day going through it and jotted down what it did well and what it botched.
First, what this project is: a pure client-side React SPA, backend is Express packaged into a single Vercel Function entry, api/index.ts plus six modules under api/lib/, database is Neon Postgres, object storage via an S3-compatible API. That’s all it is — not complicated.
 First, what it did well
 Some commits included verifiable validation results
4 of the 9 commits ended with validation results, and they carried checkable numbers.
The one wiring up object storage ended with “local end-to-end smoke passed: presign → PUT → public GET returns a 1×1 PNG” — a 1×1 PNG means it really ran the whole chain~ The one doing the existing-data migration ended with “done: 19 objects / 1.77 MB. DB has 0 data: leftovers” — how much was migrated and how much remained, both pinned down.
Of course, not every commit was like that. The validation section of the go-live acceptance commit was just one line: “Production end-to-end test passed.” — about the same as writing nothing; the deployment docs commit had a completely empty body, just a title. So don’t get too excited the moment you see a “three-part commit”…
That said, the ones with numbers were honestly better than what I write by hand…
 It wrote its own ops manual, and knew the limits of its own permissions
I can’t see anywhere in the repo that anyone asked it to write docs — it just produced a DEPLOY.md on its own, and it even covered pure infrastructure knowledge in there. For example, in the section on attaching a custom domain, it specifically flagged a warning: the CDN Proxy must be turned off and use grey cloud, because enabling the proxy prevents Vercel’s SSL certificate from getting the ACME challenge. That has nothing to do with business code — it’s pure ops experience…
At the end of the doc it also maintained a 5-item roadmap checklist of todos, which later commits kept revising — not a one-shot artifact left to rot.
Along with that came a sense of boundaries: the object storage commit explicitly noted at the end that the custom domain needed a human to attach it manually in the console, because the token it held lacked the corresponding zone permission; the next commit recorded the state after the human finished. Knowing what it can’t do and saying so honestly beats stubbornly trying anyway…
 It proactively subtracts
This one impressed me the most. It had earlier wired up a Redis service based on the tech stack I listed, then later on self-review found zero imports in the code, so it rolled back: removed the dependency, cleaned the related text out of the README and deployment docs. The closing line of that commit was: “When Redis is actually needed later, just reopen the db + add the env back, 5 minutes’ work.”
The same message also claimed it deleted envs across three environments and removed the remote Upstash instance via the management API — I can’t verify that part from the diff, since the diff only touched 5 files (.env.example, DEPLOY.md, README.md, package.json, lockfile).
“Cleaning up thoroughly” is usually what AI is worst at; most of the time it only adds, and even when it adds wrong it doesn’t dare touch it. This time at least it cleaned up the code half properly…
 It chose to build a compatibility layer instead of touching call sites
When swapping the database, the frontend had twenty-plus components using the old SDK’s .from() chained calls. It didn’t go change those twenty-plus call sites; instead it wrote an interface-compatible shim that routed requests to the self-hosted gateway, with zero changes on the caller side. There’s not much technical depth to this trick — you’d think of it after a bit of thought — but if I’d done it myself, I’d probably have dived headfirst into editing files one by one…
It also wrote whitelist validation for the gateway, and the comment was pretty amusing, verbatim:
*   - A small allowlist of (table, op) tuples is required — anything else is
*     rejected. This keeps the proxy from turning into a "drop my whole DB"
*     button.
 Now what it botched
 All green locally, dead in production
tsconfig.json enabled allowImportingTsExtensions with noEmit, so every import in the source was written with the .ts suffix, and it ran without errors locally no matter what.
But Vercel compiled the entry into .js, and from './lib/sb-shim.ts' couldn’t find the corresponding file in production at all — straight to ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND, and that’s how production went down.
The fix commit itself stated the reason: the standard ESM TS approach is to reference the .js extension, and both tsx and tsc can transparently resolve .js to the corresponding .ts source file. This time, 7 imports across 4 files were fixed (api/index.ts accounts for 4, while sb-shim.ts/auth.ts/db-proxy.ts each account for 1). Incidentally, .vercelignore was only created this time around — before that, deployment didn’t have this file at all…
Running locally doesn’t mean it’s ready to ship, especially when the shape of the build output changes…
 Hallucinations in commit messages
The commit message for the database switch said “vercel.json: cleanUrls + www→root domain 301 + 30s function timeout”, but when I used git show to look at that diff, there was no cleanUrls key in vercel.json at all. Checking the current file, it wasn’t there either — zero hits across the entire git log -S'cleanUrls' history.
Don’t fully trust a changelog written by AI — the diff is the truth…
 Editing the docs created a contradiction
In the commit that removed Redis, I also changed the README line “redirect 301 to the root domain via the config file” to “converge to the root domain via the platform’s default 308”. But the two explicit 301s for permanent: true in vercel.json had always been there — they weren’t removed.
After the change, the README and the config file were in direct conflict, and nobody could tell which one to trust…
 Credentials ended up in git history
In the “daily development” section of the deployment docs, the line for the local admin entry directly included the admin account and plaintext password (I won’t repeat the exact values), and this password was the one db:seed seeded into the database, so it’s not as harmless as “it’s just localhost anyway”. The default password in .env.example is also an obviously weak password that no one has ever changed.
What’s interesting is that the AI itself wrote as the last item on the roadmap: “Rotate credentials: JWT_SECRET / admin password — recommend rotating once deployment is stable” — it was aware, but didn’t handle it on the spot. This is probably the most typical behavior pattern of AI: it will note down the risk in the docs, and then keep writing…
 Authentication was loosened for legacy compatibility
In the gateway’s JWT verification, there was this block in the catch branch:
} catch {
  // Legacy code uses the raw user id as a "token" — accept it as a user token
  // so unmigrated frontend code keeps working until the full JWT rollout.
  const maybeId = m[1].trim();
  if (/^[0-9a-fA-F-]{32,36}$/.test(maybeId)) {
    return { user: { sub: maybeId } };
  }
}
JWT verification failed? No problem — as long as it’s a 32-36 character hex/hyphen string, it’s accepted as a valid user token. That means knowing a user’s UUID is enough to impersonate them and pass through the gateway. This too was listed as a TODO on the roadmap, but the code shipped as-is…
 A feature was downgraded into a silent no-op
The realtime channel in the frontend shim is an empty implementation, and the comment says it plainly:
*   - channel(name) — no-op shim (Realtime is on the roadmap; signaling
*     callsites in VideoChat won't throw but won't deliver either)
The call site won’t throw an error, but nothing will ever be delivered either. This kind of problem is the hardest to debug, because it pretends to be working…
 When there’s no conventions file, where do human instructions go?
Traces of the human are scattered across several commit messages: the baseline commit mentioned “the initial version generated by the PM using AI Studio”, the next one mentioned “boolean→numeric in the PM data” and “PM stale column names”, and I quoted the line “to be manually hooked up by the user in the dashboard” earlier too.
The two sentences in the Redis-removal commit that best show that “instructions were given” are: one explaining why Redis was connected in the first place — “connecting Upstash was to align with the stack you listed” — showing the tech stack was specified by a human. The other is “Left: task 8 (VideoChat signaling) renamed to generic ‘Realtime alternative’”.
In other words, a numbered task list existed. But it’s not in the repo — grep across the whole codebase finds no task 8. It only lived in the conversation context, and once the session closed, it was gone…
This is probably the direct reason why, later on, I insisted on leaving a conventions file in the repo no matter what — even if it’s just one line, at least it won’t evaporate along with the session…
 Summing it up in a table
After going through these 9 commits, I can roughly map out the boundaries of what “AI working alone” can do:



What it does well
What it doesn’t




Scaffolding, boilerplate code
Security boundaries (auth, credentials)


Compatibility layers / shims, avoiding large-scale changes to call sites
Cross-file consistency (docs vs config)


Ops runbooks, even writing about infrastructure pitfalls
Its own changelog (hallucinates)


Migration scripts: dry-run by default, only actually runs with --apply, idempotent
Risks it notes down never get fixed later



That migration script deserves a special mention: by default it only prints a dry-run, and only actually uploads when --apply is added, and objects already starting with http are skipped directly, so running it repeatedly won’t cause problems. If I wrote this design myself, it’d come out about the same…
 By the way: a comment written specifically for agents to read
While going through vite.config.ts, I came across a comment:
server: {
  // HMR is disabled in AI Studio via DISABLE_HMR env var.
  // Do not modify—file watching is disabled to prevent flickering during agent edits.
  hmr: process.env.DISABLE_HMR !== 'true',
},
Meaning: file watching was turned off by an environment variable, because the high-frequency writes from an agent editing files would make HMR flicker like crazy.
To be clear, this one wasn’t written by it; git log -- app/vite.config.ts only has the baseline import, a scaffolding comment that shipped with the initial version when the PM exported it from AI Studio, and nobody has touched it since. Conversely, that’s even more telling: it’s not some agent leaving a note for itself — the toolchain is already adapting by default to the scenario of “an AI is modifying these files.” In the past, this kind of comment was written for the next person to take over; now it’s also, in passing, written for the next model to take over…
Anyway, the conclusion is that it won’t stop on its own — someone, or a CI, has to force it to pause…

title: When Multiple AIs Write Code Together, the Boundaries I Draw for Them
content:
Lately, across a few projects, the same repo has been modified by two AI coding tools at once, plus a few people pushing code themselves… At first I figured it was no big deal — it’s all just writing code, right? But after stumbling through it, I found the problems were almost never in the code itself; they were in collaboration mechanics — “who read which set of rules,” “who can touch what on the machine.” Here I’m writing down the boundaries I eventually drew.
 First, a twist: the so-called “multiple parties”
Going through another one of my repos, I ran into something amusing. git shortlog -sn turned up two lines with two names, looking like two people pushing; a check of the email addresses showed they were the same person — the extra one was just my account name from clicking merge in the web UI. And of the 78 commits, 63 carry Co-Authored-By: Claude — the real “multiple parties” was never multiple people at all, it was one person plus several AI sessions. The traces of parallelism weren’t in .claude/worktrees/ either (that directory is empty, and git worktree list has only the single line for the main repo), but in the branch names: five branches with the claude/ prefix, and once two were open at the same time and eventually merged into each other.
So these boundaries below — I originally thought I was drawing them for people, but looking back, they’re mostly for “me and the several sessions I spun up myself.” Sessions share no memory whatsoever, which is worse than dealing with a colleague.
 Rule files split
One team repo had fairly complete conventions — a prohibition list, version differences, commit rules — but all of it lived under one AI tool’s rules directory, and all of it was set to always apply. The problem: the other tool doesn’t read that directory at all; on its side there’s just one line of import plus the generic prompt injected by the scaffold. The two AIs have completely different context — one knows “there are other production projects on this machine,” the other knows nothing…
My own repo has a ready-made cautionary example too: acg-site maintains three sets of convention files at once, and I only updated one. The version numbers and command descriptions in the other two sat frozen at their old values — I tallied up the gory details in the post about convention files, so I won’t repeat it here.
The conclusion is blunt: keep exactly one source of truth, and point everything else at it with import. The CLAUDE.md in vns-next and thdl are each a single line; the content all lives in AGENTS.md. Change one place and both sides take effect at once — no room for drift.
But that trick only solves “one person maintaining two copies.” The multi-AI scenario adds another layer: the other tool simply doesn’t read the file you’re pointing at. So what really needs confirming isn’t “are the rules complete,” but “what actually got loaded into each agent at startup” — and there’s no shortcut; you have to try it tool by tool.
 Boundary one: don’t touch anything else on the machine
The team’s machine that runs the agents has several projects running at once, so we wrote a dedicated “production environment safety constraints” rule and set it to always apply. The prohibitions go roughly like this:

Don’t kill processes by port number
No batch process-killing commands like killall / pkill
Don’t modify anything under system-level config directories
Don’t sudo any command
Port conflicts get reported to a human only, never handled by the agent itself
Database operations are limited to this project’s own database
Check the blast radius before acting; if in doubt, ask first

I now copy these onto every machine that has an agent installed… When an agent sees a port is taken, its first instinct is to kill the process holding it, with no idea it’s the neighboring project’s production service.
 Boundary two: don’t write APIs from memory
This pitfall is far too common — the API in the training data and the version in your package.json are not remotely the same thing… I’ve given examples of how to turn version differences into ❌→✅ comparison tables in two other posts, so here I’ll only cover the half that matters more for collaboration.
In that rules file the comparison table actually comes last; what opens it is a three-step SOP: first resolve-library-id, then query-docs, write code based on what the docs say, and spell out which scenarios “require checking the docs.” Process first, error examples second — that order matters: error examples are finite and expire, while process can cover the libraries you didn’t anticipate. You can’t list every library’s pitfalls for everyone.
There’s also a lazier route: the newer scaffolds inject a block into the repo themselves — "don’t trust your training data, go read the docs in node_modules" — complete with BEGIN/END markers, plainly meant for tools to overwrite. Nobody has to write the convention, maintenance cost drops to zero; take the freebies where you can~
Conversely, prohibitions need reasons. In the docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:115 of that repo I mentioned earlier, tucked into the tech stack table, there’s a line: client types are generated from the backend OpenAPI, do not introduce tRPC/Prisma, and the reason follows right after — the backend is a REST service in Rust axum, so a JS backend contract simply doesn’t exist. Those two are the default answers in the TS ecosystem, and an AI will install them without thinking; writing only “tRPC is forbidden” won’t stop it, because the next session can always decide the rule is outdated. With the reason attached, it’s not a commandment but a factual judgment. The same document’s :148 even limits the mirror’s permissions: the other side mirrors the DTOs with pydantic “for submission only, do not persist the structure” — a copy is allowed, but the copy must never become the source of truth.
 Boundary three: large AI changes must be humanly reviewable
(This is part 1 of 3 of the same post.)
In another team’s repo, the PR template has a line of comment at the top that goes something like this: in scenarios where multiple humans work alongside AI, the PR is the only human gate before bad code reaches production, so please fill out the checklist honestly. Two items in the self-test checklist are aimed squarely at AI: one requires controlling PR size and splitting up large changes, the reason being that a human has to be able to read it in a few minutes; the other requires the submitter to have gone through the AI-written parts line by line and to own them.
Those two items are more useful than any lint rule. Lint only catches things at the syntax level; it can’t catch logic that runs fine but is wrong…
 Gates in pre-commit or in CI
That same repo’s choice is to run the full type check + full unit tests in pre-commit. The reasoning is written in a comment in the config: CI only triggers when merging to main, while the staging branch is push-only with no PRs, so if you relied on CI alone the breakage wouldn’t surface until merge…
One detail worth copying—the type check is whole-project, and you can’t just feed it a single file, so the hook returns a fixed command and simply ignores the matched filenames. There’s also a secret-scanning layer on top: local scans the staged changes, CI scans the whole repo.
Comparing against a few of my own repos, the gate strength varies wildly:



Project
Gate
Strength




acg-site
CI seven steps (install deps → db:generate → Biome format check → ESLint → tsc → unit tests → build) + pre-commit running lint-staged
★★★★★


bbps
lint added --max-warnings 0, but typecheck wasn’t added until a month later
★★


vns-next
Just one "check": "biome check && tsc --noEmit", no CI, no hook
★★


acgn-flow
Doesn’t even have a typecheck script—the only static check is eslint .
★



The bbps case illustrates it best: lint was already there in 2025-11, --max-warnings 0 wasn’t added until 2026-02, and typecheck and check didn’t make it into package.json until 1d953fe9 a month later… The very day they were added, a type problem got caught—the third-party CSS import in comments-section.tsx that has no type declaration needed an inline comment exemption on the spot.
That repo also has a gate I hadn’t thought of, one that guards cross-language contracts specifically: CI re-runs code generation and then diffs the result against what’s committed.
- run: pnpm gen:client
- name: Fail if OpenAPI/TS client drifted from committed source
  run: git diff --exit-code apps/api/openapi.json packages/api-client/src/schema.d.ts
One byte off and it’s red. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:176 writing “change the backend = change one place, clients update automatically” is a principle; these two lines are what make it impossible to violate. Same playbook as bbps: the commit that introduced this gate also says “restore a few endpoints that had drifted earlier”—and it caught pre-existing drift the moment it shipped.
By the way, here’s how Biome and ESLint split duties without stepping on each other: biome.json:20-25 in acg-site turns off the linter and assist entirely, so Biome handles formatting only and all linting goes to ESLint; CLAUDE.md:109 spells this out too, so that next time the AI doesn’t see Biome and go turn the linter back on~
 28 minutes after the blow-up, the lessons became a script
This is the most beautiful passage I saw in that repo. That afternoon the backend crashed first: a comment structure referencing itself (replies: Vec<CommentOut>), perfectly legal in Rust’s type system, with cargo build, clippy -D warnings, and cargo test all green, but at startup generating the OpenAPI spec recursed infinitely, overflowed the stack, and entered a crash loop, going from 502 all the way to the whole site returning 500—a purely documentation-layer thing took down production. Nine minutes later, the second one: a newly added top-level page wasn’t in the middleware whitelist and got treated as a localized route by i18n, causing a runtime 404, while next build showed the route existed and CI was all green.
Nineteen minutes after that, a third commit turned these two lessons into two smoke tests in the deploy script, 13 lines of shell:
# ①：真跑一次二进制，拦「build 全绿但启动就崩」
SQLX_OFFLINE=true timeout 30 target/release/api --openapi >/dev/null 2>&1 \
  || { echo "✗ 冒烟失败——中止部署，未传镜像"; exit 1; }

# ②：顶层页必须在 middleware 白名单里，否则运行时 404
for _d in apps/web/src/app/*/; do
  _n=$(basename "$_d"); case "$_n" in "[locale]"|dash) continue ;; esac
  [ -f "${_d}page.tsx" ] || continue
  grep -q "\"/$_n\"" apps/web/src/middleware.ts || { echo "✗ /$_n 未放行"; exit 1; }
done
Crude as dirt—one runs the binary, the other greps—but it’s second-scale, deterministic, needs no service started or database connection, and the interception point is before the image is pushed: a bad artifact never even leaves the local machine. All those tsc, clippy, and lint layers are more and more formal, but the two times the site actually got taken down, it was these thirteen lines that stopped it.
 How to review AI output
Two examples from over there left a deep impression. One was a deliberately adversarial review after a big AI rewrite, which in one go surfaced a dozen confirmed defects: server-side request forgery, where a configurable address got fetched directly by the server; a bulk import that wasn’t atomic, so failed records were counted as successes too; a data dashboard that mixed rolling 168-hour windows with calendar-day seven-day windows; cache writes that weren’t tagged, so later reads got stale data. Not a single one of these could tsc or lint catch.
Another: a state value was never written by any code, so a multi-step progress bar could never reach the final step—it rendered four circles, but the state advanced at most to the third. Querying production for the number of rows using that value returned 0.
There was also a rather rare one: the requirement was barely described, so the AI made a defensive interpretation and even wrote in the commit message, “if later specs don’t match this interpretation, this change amounts to an unrelated action.” That’s rarer than getting it right~
There are also cases in my own repos that were rescued by human review. In acg-site's c2193c3: a single PR changed the local-dev fallback port from :3000 to :4000, but the other 8 occurrences of .env.example within the same PR still said :3000. The verdict was “dirty changes committed along the way”; reverting kept the whole repo consistent.
The repo where AI accounts for 80% does it more carefully: multiple perspectives independently review the same code, and the output is a numbered, graded list (H1/M1/L1). The conclusion isn’t binary pass-or-fail either; there’s a go-with-notes tier—mergeable, but these items need follow-up. What it catches are all timing issues that lint can’t reach: check-then-write races overwriting each other under concurrency, effect re-runs clobbering unsaved edits, optimistic updates failing without rollback.
The flip side is right here too: this whole process can’t be found anywhere in the repo—no persistent rules file, no CI job, no agent definition. It lives only in a few commit messages. No matter how rigidly structured they are, how many “Lesson:” sections and reproduction commands they include, the next session only gets them if it happens to dig through git log.
 A few side effects of parallel worktrees
In thdl, git worktree list shows three lines: the main repo is on main, and the other two are .claude/worktrees/heuristic-bardeen-567381 and .claude/worktrees/sweet-poincare-f3b7bc. The random-background feature was built in one of them. Handy, but there are three side effects.
 A worktree is a full checkout, so lint and formatters will scan it
acg-site's eslint.config.mjs:22-25 just adds it to the ignore list:
// IDE local history
".history/**",
// Claude Code worktrees
".claude/**",
biome.json's files.includes excludes it the same way. Without that, running lint once means scanning the same code twice…
 Multiple lockfiles make the bundler pick the wrong workspace root (worktrees are only one cause)
bbps’s 449d72b3 added turbopack: { root: process.cwd() } to next.config.ts, with the comment “avoid Turbopack root inference warnings when there are multiple lockfiles”—at that point it had nothing to do with worktrees. home’s 54b4590 hit the same class of problem but in the opposite direction: it had to stop Next from inferring the workspace root from a pnpm-lock.yaml in the parent directory. Worktrees are just one more source.
 Easy to commit by mistake
home once committed a subdirectory under .claude/worktrees/ as a gitlink, dragging in 12 .history/ files and a .env along with it—a classic byproduct of git add -A, with not a word about it in the commit message. Later .history was added to .gitignore, but gitignore doesn’t untrack already-tracked files, so that batch is still sitting in the repo to this day. What the hell—I tell myself every time not to use -A…
So remember to add worktree directories to .gitignore and the various ignore lists at the same time; miss one and it’s a trap~
In the end, none of this is a code problem—it’s all about who reads what and who can touch what. No matter how many tools there are, these two things still have to be decided by a human~

title: Getting Claude to Make Fewer Data-Layer Mistakes: Prisma, Drizzle, and a Few Structured Practices
content:
Recent projects each used Prisma, Drizzle, or skipped the ORM entirely and wrote raw SQL.
The same AI makes completely different mistakes on each of the three—that surprised me quite a bit… On Prisma it writes “the correct way from the previous major version”; on Drizzle it gets stuck on types and API signatures; on raw SQL it has no idea what limitations that driver has.
Here I’ll note down a few fallback practices I use along the schema-to-migration chain—just notes for myself.
Prisma 7 / Drizzle 0.45 / Next 16. If the versions don’t line up, all the approaches below will change.

 A few spots in Prisma 7 where AI is guaranteed to write it wrong
The CLAUDE.md:18-25 in that acg-site repo has a section literally titled “Key Version Differences (Common AI Mistakes)”. Of the six bullets, only one is Prisma-related:

The Prisma 7 generator is "prisma-client" (not "prisma-client-js"), import path @/generated/prisma/client

One bullet crammed in two things. The ❌→✅ comparison table at the end of .cursor/rules/library-versions.mdc in the same repo splits it into items 3 and 4, writing it out separately again (that repo maintains three sets of convention files at once—I did the cost accounting for writing it that way in the post about convention files, so here I’ll only pick the data-layer-related ones).
It looks redundant, but it’s actually very necessary. Because these two things aren’t a case of “AI can’t do it” but of “AI remembers the old one”.
If you don’t hard-code it, it will guess from memory 100% of the time—it never fails.
I’ll add one of my own: since Prisma 7, the connection string moved from the schema to prisma.config.ts, and the validation in that file is usually written to throw unconditionally.
That’s how prisma.config.ts:5-8 in vns-next looks:
const url = process.env.DATABASE_URL;
if (!url) {
  throw new Error("DATABASE_URL is not defined");
}
The consequence is that during the Docker build you must feed in a placeholder value, even though prisma generate never connects to a database at all—that’s where those two lines of SKIP_ENV_VALIDATION=1 plus a fake connection string in the image come from; I pasted the original text in the self-hosting post.
What you need to note is the direction of causality: the Dockerfile isn’t written wrong—it’s the unconditional throw in prisma.config.ts that ropes the build phase in too.
Any library that does validation at the top level of a config file has this problem; Prisma is just the one I ran into recently.
These all fall under “the training data has the old syntax”. Writing them into CLAUDE.md is the highest-value kind of convention—one line saves you half an hour.
 db push can’t create native SQL indexes
This pitfall isn’t the AI’s fault, but the AI won’t proactively warn you about it either.
The search in vns-next uses the pg_trgm extension plus three GIN indexes: fuzzy title, alias array containment, fuzzy tag name. prisma db push won’t create any of these for you—it only syncs what can be expressed in the schema.
So I put them separately in a scripts/db/indexes.sql, with the first line of comments at the top reading “Prisma schema cannot declare trgm/expression indexes; run manually after db:push”.
More importantly, how to verify. The line recorded in the body of commit 35659c4 is “pg_trgm search (EXPLAIN verified index usage)”.
A query running successfully doesn’t mean it used the index—a full table scan also returns correct results, just slowly. For this kind of thing you have to look at the execution plan, not at whether the endpoint returns 200.
 A few friction points on the Drizzle side
The thdl side uses Drizzle + postgres.js, and the friction points are a whole different batch.
 Connection pool
Dev hot reload keeps creating new connections over and over and leaking them all; you have to attach a globalThis singleton.
This is a pitfall very familiar to Prisma users; switching to Drizzle you still have to hand-write it once (src/lib/db/index.ts:8-13):
declare global {
  var __thdl_pg: ReturnType<typeof postgres> | undefined;
}

const client = globalThis.__thdl_pg ?? postgres(connectionString, { max: 10 });
if (process.env.NODE_ENV !== "production") globalThis.__thdl_pg = client;
 Enum columns meet searchParams
What comes up from the URL is always string, while the pgEnum column is a union of 9 literals—there’s no clean conversion path in between.
In the end the code was written like this (src/app/(site)/resources/page.tsx:21):
cat ? eq(resources.category, cat as "music") : undefined
It just picks an arbitrary member and casts to it. It works, but it throws away the validation responsibility entirely; to actually do it properly you’d have to pass it through zod’s enum first.
I’ll jot this down for now, haven’t touched it…
 Version differences again
The second parameter of Drizzle’s table definition changed starting from 0.36 to return an array instead of an object. thdl has 0.45.2 installed; see src/lib/db/schema.ts:113-117 for the syntax:
(t) => [
  index("resources_status_created_idx").on(t.status, t.createdAt),
  index("resources_category_idx").on(t.category),
]
The AI will most likely write it as => ({ ... }) for you—same nature as those two Prisma points. When checking the changelog, remember not to look at the wrong version; you won’t find this one in 0.45.
 And one more that’s not a code problem
What I run locally is pnpm db:push; the steps the README gives everyone else are also pnpm db:push; and in the drizzle/ directory there’s still just one baseline migration to this day.
package.json:14 does define db:migrate, but grepping the whole repo turns up no call site. The deploy side is even more blunt: deploy/ contains nothing but a Caddyfile and a systemd unit, ExecStart is just node server.js, and the database is never touched at all.
In other words, there’s no versioned record of how the schema evolved step by step; it all depends on push aligning things on the spot.
The database is still small, so pushing all at once really is fine for now. But once the table structure gets complicated, or a second person actually has to deploy a copy, that debt comes due… I know it, I just haven’t gotten to it yet.
 Wiring the ORM and the auth library takes manual alignment
thdl uses better-auth’s drizzleAdapter, which expects four tables: user / session / account / verification.
But the table names in your own schema aren’t necessarily those, so you have to map them by hand (src/lib/auth.ts:8-16):
database: drizzleAdapter(db, {
  provider: "pg",
  schema: {
    user: schema.users,
    session: schema.sessions,
    account: schema.accounts,
    verification: schema.verifications,
  },
}),
The AI doesn’t get this wrong because it’s dumb, but because it has no way to know out of thin air what your tables are called. This is exactly the kind of part where a human has to pin things down first and only then let it do the wiring.
A fossil worth mentioning in passing: the allowlist in that repo’s .claude/settings.local.json has two commands back to back — delete the old auth library’s catch-all route directory, create the new auth library’s catch-all route directory.
An entire library swap got recorded in full like that, and in the end the route file is only 4 lines long. Hilarious.
 Migration scripts must be idempotent, and they need unit tests
When vns-next migrated from the old Hugo site to Postgres, the first line of the header comment in scripts/migrate-content.ts states the strategy: “Idempotent and re-runnable: upsert Work/Page by primary key; deleteMany DownloadLink then insert; clear then insert SiteLink/TeamMember/DlEntry.”
If it dies partway through, you just run it again — that premise made the whole migration far easier.
I pulled the parsing logic into a standalone module, scripts/lib/parse.ts, with 31 test cases across 6 describe blocks; the acceptance line in the body of commit 35659c4 is simply “all 31 tests green.”
The scariest thing in data migration isn’t a crash, it’s a silent error. A field shifted out of place, a date off by a day — everything runs green and you still can’t see it. Pure functions plus unit tests are the only thing holding the line.
The timezone pitfall deserves its own section. The default schema in js-yaml parses a timezone-less string like date: 2024-07-31 03:56:40 straight into Date, computed as UTC, and the timezone is wrong right there.
The fix is to switch to JSON_SCHEMA so it stays a string, then parse it yourself with +08:00. The comment in scripts/lib/parse.ts:12-13 reads:

js-yaml is a dependency of gray-matter, so we reuse it directly here.
Using JSON_SCHEMA keeps date: 2024-07-31 03:56:40 as a string (the default schema parses it into a Date as UTC, which gets the timezone wrong)

The record counts need to be checkable too. After the migration, the body of commit 35659c4 recorded work=145 / tag=247 / download_link=2307 / page=22 / dl_entry=89.
deploy/README.md:35 picked the first three and wrote them into the import notes, with a verification SQL given separately on line 48: after import, select count(*) from work should be 145. With that one line, re-running it on another machine feels safe.
One last point that’s easy to overlook: encode/decode functions shared between migration scripts and the frontend must be pulled out into a zero-dependency module.
The header of vns-next’s src/lib/download-label.ts:1-3 says:
/**
 * DownloadLink.label 的编码/解码 —— 纯函数、零依赖
 *（迁移脚本与前端共用；不要在这里引入任何 node/解析库依赖）
 */
It started with commit 404a769: “extract splitLabel into a zero-dependency module to keep gray-matter out of the client bundle.”
Once a shared function casually imports a parsing library, it crawls all the way into the client bundle through the import chain, and nothing can stop it.
 When you don’t use an ORM
Another project skipped the ORM entirely and just writes raw SQL through a serverless Postgres HTTP driver.
The complexity you save gets handed straight back to your migration scripts:

That driver executes only one statement at a time, so the migration script has to implement its own semicolon-splitting state machine, and also handle dollar-quoted blocks and semicolons inside strings
Bulk writes must be combined into a single unnest upsert. Under an HTTP driver every statement is a separate network round trip, and once the row count grows the latency gets ugly
Migrations use plain filename ordinals and re-run in full every time, relying on the SQL being idempotent — there isn’t even a migration state table

That last one is actually the most worry-free. With no state table, there’s no “state table doesn’t match the real schema” problem — the hardest kind to track down.
 A few habits I have now



Approach
What it solves
Frequency




Lock down the schema before letting AI write queries
Stops it from guessing fields from memory
★★★★★


Migration scripts must be idempotent and re-runnable
If it fails midway, you can just run it again
★★★★★


Extract parsing/encoding into pure functions with unit tests
Silent errors are the scariest thing in data migrations
★★★★


Keep native indexes in a separate SQL file
Neither push nor generate will create them for you
★★★


Feed a fake connection string at build time
The Docker build layer has no database
★★★



That’s it for now — I’ll add more next time I switch ORMs~

title: 188 Players, 0 That Play Sound: An Old Bug Exposed by a Theme Upgrade
content:
The Butterfly release notes for the jump from 5.6.1 to 5.7.0 state one thing plainly: built-in APlayer/Meting support has been removed. After upgrading, the aplayerInject config stopped working, and the related entries in layout/includes/third-party/aplayer.pug and plugins.yml vanished along with it.
/music/ holds 188 <meting-js>, and inject also contains one fixed player. The tags themselves are still there, but the script injection is gone, so the page just shows a row of empty custom elements.
At this point the story should be “the upgrade broke the players, so roll back or hand-write the inject.” But I measured the baseline first, and the result was a little surprising.
 Before the upgrade, it was already zero
meting-js defaults to MetingJS’s built-in backend api.i-meto.com. That service is already dead: its responses carry no CORS headers, so every browser request fails. In other words, not a single player on the live site had been rendering for a while — nobody had just bothered to count.
The theme upgrade isn’t the culprit; it merely pried up a floorboard that had rotted long ago. That distinction matters: roll back the version and the page returns to a state where “the player code looks like it’s there, but the count is still zero,” and you keep assuming it’s fine.
 Hand-writing the inject: order is a hard constraint
The fix is to include them yourself, in order, inside inject:
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://registry.npmmirror.com/aplayer/latest/files/dist/APlayer.min.css" media="print" onload="this.media='all'">
...
<script src="https://registry.npmmirror.com/aplayer/latest/files/dist/APlayer.min.js"></script>
<script>window.meting_api="https://meting-api.saop.cc/api?server=:server&type=:type&id=:id&r=:r"</script>
<script src="https://registry.npmmirror.com/meting/latest/files/dist/Meting.min.js"></script>
window.meting_api must be set before Meting.min.js; one line later and it has no effect. For CSS, use media="print" + onload to switch to all, which doesn’t block first paint.
 The pjax glue script was actually dead code
The theme also used to have a pjax hook that destroyed and rebuilt destroyAplayer on page switches. Looking into APlayer 1.10.1, window.aplayers is no longer maintained, so that destroyAplayer had nothing to destroy in the first place.
MetingJS v2, meanwhile, is a standard custom element, so on page switches it rebuilds and destroys itself via connectedCallback / disconnectedCallback. So the conclusion this time is no glue: let the element own its own lifecycle.
 After fixing it, count
Measured after the change:

players rendered: 0 → 167/188;
after a pjax round trip, every in-page player is rebuilt;
the fixed player stays the same DOM node throughout, with playback uninterrupted.

Of the remaining 21, twenty are type="album" — the self-hosted Meting API doesn’t support that type yet and returns 400. The other one or two are intermittent failures caused by rate limiting under 188 concurrent requests. Both are on the API server side and unrelated to this repo; the commit message says as much, and I didn’t count them as “fixed.”
167/188 isn’t a perfect score, but it’s a number you can re-check: render count, pjax round trip, and fixed-node identity each have their own observation point.
 When upgrading, separate the two accounts first
The most expensive part of a dependency upgrade isn’t editing config; it’s being able to say clearly, before the upgrade, what things actually look like right now. This time the baseline was a single sentence — zero — and it decided every judgment that followed:

if the zero had been caused by the upgrade, I should suspect the 5.7.0 changes, or even roll back;
if the zero was an old debt and the upgrade merely made it visible, I should fix the backend and the injection order, not roll back.

Along the way I also cleared out a piece of dead code. Had I been lazy and copied destroyAplayer verbatim into the new inject, it would have “worked” too — it would just do something useless against an empty array on every page switch, and the next person would have even less chance of seeing why it exists.
Measure what things looked like before, then decide what the upgrade broke.

title: After Moving Off Vercel, the Safety Nets the Platform Provided Started Showing One by One
content:
On September 29 and 30, twenty-one commits over two days moved nav-site from Vercel + Neon to a Singapore VPS: Cloudflare Tunnel in, the origin exposes no public ports, postgres binds only to 127.0.0.1:5432, the app runs in Docker Compose, and builds are done on the server with a dedicated buildx builder.
The migration ultimately succeeded. But those earlier commits were almost all patching the same category of thing: assumptions the platform used to make on my behalf. This post records them in order of discovery, not in commit order.
 One hop lands on 0.0.0.0:3000
Before switching production, I tested in preview: the 302 landing point for /r/<渠道码> was https://0.0.0.0:3000/, and the same applied to the callback redirects after successful and failed Google login. If the redirect entry point had only been discovered on production switch day, every short link on the site would have broken at once.
The root cause is in attachRequestMeta of next-server.js: in standalone mode, next-server holds the hostname/port it listens on and prioritizes them when constructing the request URL, so the experimental.trustHostHeader branch is never reached. On Vercel, the platform automatically trusts Host (config.js is enabled at hasNextSupport), so this was never exposed before the migration. In testing, neither Host nor X-Forwarded-Host affected req.url; only the protocol followed X-Forwarded-Proto.
The fix is a newly added lib/public-origin.ts: take the Host header (the origin is reachable only through the tunnel, and Cloudflare writes Host based on the domain the visitor requested), and for the protocol accept only https from X-Forwarded-Proto. Deliberately do not trust X-Forwarded-Host—visitors can supply it themselves, Cloudflare passes it through unchanged, and trusting it is an open redirect.
I also replaced openapi.json and llms.txt along the way: they used to prioritize reading XFH to build the site root, which is forgeable after self-hosting, and the endpoint is cached at the edge for an hour, which amounts to cache poisoning.
 Same commit, prod and preview fight over one image tag
Both sides build nav-site:<sha>. But the same commit does not produce identical artifacts on both sides: the database connected at build time, prerendered data, and NEXT_PUBLIC_* can all differ. Whichever builds later takes over the tag—in testing, when production built later, the preview container’s image became an unnamed sha256:…; conversely, a production restart or rollback would end up on a build containing preview data.
Changed to nav-site:<env>-<sha>, so build, release, rollback, and cleanup all carry an environment prefix. Image identity cannot rely on commit alone; things with different artifacts should not share one name.
 Secrets don’t enter the cache key
When releasing via CI on the VPS for the first time, between two commits only the deploy/ script changed (it does not enter the build context), and the whole pipeline hit cache and completed in 5 seconds. The cache itself was not the problem, but it exposed a quieter hazard: build-time environment variables are injected via BuildKit secrets, and the secret contents do not participate in the cache key. When only env changes and the code does not, pnpm build hits the old cache and the new NEXT_PUBLIC_* silently fails to take effect.
The fix is that deploy.sh passes the first 16 characters of the build env file’s sha256 as a build arg, and echo it in Dockerfile. As soon as env changes, the cache is invalidated.
 EXIT trap references a local variable; a successful release exits 1
The EXIT trap in cmd_build_deploy / cmd_migrate used a function-local variable. The trap only fires when the script exits after the function returns normally; under set -u it reports “unbound”, turning a successful release into exit code 1—CI then marks every success red. After cleanup completes, trap - EXIT is removed.
 pg-verify treats “empty vs. empty” as a match
When running the import against Neon for the first time, the source database failed to connect because of a certificate parameter. Yet pg-verify output “✓ sequence values match”—both sides were empty results, and since the table loop was empty there was no ✗ either. Although the script ultimately exited non-zero because of set -e, it reached no clear conclusion; on the night of the switch, it could easily have been read as a pass.
Now it first confirms both ends are reachable and that the source database really has tables under public; otherwise it exits 2 immediately. One more note: for libpq with sslmode=verify-full, sslrootcert=system must be added; Node’s pg driver does not recognize this parameter, so the connection string used by the app should contain only sslmode=verify-full.
 Backups in a public bucket
The original recommendation was to create a new private backup bucket; later we decided to use the primary bucket nav-bucket directly—it has a public CDN domain attached, is publicly readable, and its object keys contain timestamps that make them guessable. The database contains user emails, password hashes, and partner keys; uploading it in plaintext would be equivalent to making it public.
So everything is age-encrypted before upload; if BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT is empty, the upload is refused outright (fail-closed), and ciphertext is placed under a prefix with a random suffix. The decryption private key is in /opt/nav-site/env/backup-age.key; a separate copy must be stored outside the machine: if the machine is lost entirely, the backups on R2 can only be decrypted with it.
 Splitting one key into three
CHANNEL_REPORT_SECRET, USER_SESSION_SECRET, ADMIN_SESSION_SECRET, and CRON_SECRET all used to fall back to the same value, so the validity of externally shared links ended up tied to a key whose name gave no hint of the connection. When we split them apart during the migration, deploy.sh refuses to publish if any one of them is missing.
Among them, changing CHANNEL_REPORT_SECRET invalidates every externally shared link and QR code already sent to partners, so it must be stored somewhere other than the server; the others can be rotated at any time, and the only cost is that whoever happens to be logging in fails once. Keys that can be rotated at any time and keys that can’t must not look the same.
 A few more that look harmless but bite

fail2ban on this machine bans you for 24 hours after 3 authentication failures. When you can’t connect, find out why first — don’t go guessing usernames.
sshd has port forwarding disabled, so migrations, script runs, and database queries all happen on the server itself; there is no SSH tunnel to fall back on.
The migrator keeps no record table. It reruns everything by filename every time, so migration files must be idempotent.
A deploy normally takes about 7 seconds with zero failed requests, and a bad version that won’t start is rolled back automatically. But Docker’s service-name resolution ignores health status: a version that can listen on the port yet returns wrong responses will receive roughly half the traffic during the health-check window, which lasts up to 30 seconds. That boundary is written into the runbook; we didn’t pretend it doesn’t exist.
Run a restore drill at least once a quarter — a backup that has never been restored isn’t a backup.

 The defaults after the move
Vercel trusted the Host for you, gave every build its own identity, guaranteed that your backup bucket was private, and said “consistent” for you when a result was empty. Self-hosting doesn’t make these things disappear; it turns them from the platform’s defaults into your own defaults: one publicOrigin, one <env>-<sha> label, one sha256 build arg, two preflight checks, and one age public key.
What really matters in a migration checklist is never the commands — it’s whether each of these assumptions has been caught, one by one.

title: The Client CSV Is the Single Source of Truth: C1 to C68, Handing Back Each Value One by One
content:
To set the context: this is my own Boom Beach private server, client version 57.135. Besides the server, there’s a webclient that rebuilds base rendering and editing in the browser. The client ships its own complete set of csv/ — buildings, obstacles, decorations, traps, entries, globals — and even “how much gold it takes to remove this rock, how much wood it drops, what Headquarters level you need” is written in there.
These things used to be copied separately into the engine and into the shell. Over the past ten days I deleted the copied parts one by one and switched to reading the tables directly; the changes are numbered C35 through C68. This post isn’t a replay in commit order — it just picks a few things worth recording: why reading the table is non-negotiable, how to turn “did it actually read” into a test that goes red, and why you can’t invent things the table doesn’t contain.
 The cost of hand-copying isn’t “getting it wrong once”
The worst form of hand-copying isn’t a mistake — it’s copying something correctly and then nobody knowing it has gone stale. A cell changes in the client table, the copy in the engine doesn’t move with it, and the symptom usually shows up far from the source: water color off by 1, obstacle clearing not charging anything, the same decoration placeable a hundred times — and the tests all green.
A few of the spots cleaned up this time are pretty typical:



Location
True value in the table
Behavior when hand-copied




src/terrain.h
globals.csv three water palettes, 12 cells total
a pixel comparison only reports “water in some region is off by 1”


removeAt
ClearCost of obstacles.csv 600…25000
free deletion, no gold charged, no loot dropped


Decoration placement
MaxCount of decos.csv is only 0/1/2
duplicate at will, the cap is never shown


Attack panel
buildings.csv four columns of status effects
17 objects, 78 levels carrying values, the panel is completely blank



So from C44 onward I changed approach: values come only from the table, the engine only does addition and clamping, and the shell doesn’t make up numbers of its own. The only exception is the seed, which is flagged separately in a comment.
 First, make “did it read or not” decidable
Reading the table isn’t hard. What’s hard is knowing, next session, that this cell was really read. C44 started from a shipped texts_patch.csv: of 6 rows, 2 cells are non-empty, and one of those TIDs doesn’t exist in texts.csv at all — the client only displays it thanks to a patch. After filling it in, the artifact gained a verifiable section:
window.hbTextMeta.patch = { present: true, rows: 6, cells: 2, sha256: '3e815929…' }
TEXTS OK in the acceptance chain prints these two numbers and the patch’s sha256. C45 goes further with tools/globals_check.py, pinning the three hand-copied water palettes in src/terrain.h back cell by cell against csv/globals.csv, checking field order along the way.
This chain now runs to PARITY OK ×96, three browser paths at 413/413/366 ✓, and ENGINE TEXTS OK scans 27 source files and 949 string literals, where non-ASCII must be 0. It can’t catch “read the wrong column”, but it can catch “forgot to read”.
 What the table doesn’t have: copy it, don’t invent it
C63 was the hardest one. StatusEffectType has four kinds — Fire, Stun, SpeedBoost, Panic;SpeedBoost — with the four columns split into parallel segments by semicolons, and the value of Barbed Wire_lvl1 is -750 (a negative number means a slowdown). The type word has no exact cell in texts.csv: only 速度加成 hits a row, everything else is zero hits.
So I made a very crude decision: keep the type word’s raw value from the table — no translation, no sentence building. The prompt string likewise follows the client’s single TID_STATBAR_HINT_BURN_DAMAGE (“Set the target on fire”), even though it doesn’t quite fit Stun — that is simply what sits in that spot in the client.
C61 illustrates it even better. Obstacle clearing has a whole flow of copy in the client: TID_POPUP_CLEAR_OBSTACLE_TITLE, TID_AVAILABLE_LOOT, TID_CAN_NOT_CLEAR_OBSTACLE, and even "You need to reach Headquarters level " is already written. The shell used to call only hb.remove, so none of those four strings was ever used. After switching to table reads, gold deduction, loot crediting, and the level gate all follow the rows; ClearTimeSeconds has nine rows that are all 0, and they’re still read as-is, with no countdown scheduled.
C68’s decoration cap has only three tiers, 0/1/2. No_Decos is 0 and Speaker is 2. 250 items have Unlockable = TRUE (free once unlocked), and the 11 left blank are exactly the paid items carrying BuildCost. The shell now counts the current number, shows TID_BUILDING_CAP_REACHED verbatim once you hit the cap, and actually charges money for placing paid items.
 An easter egg: the client left a TID language of its own
While going through csv/locales.csv for C49, I noticed a row in the language list literally named TID, which declares nothing but ShowTID = TRUE, and whose font is empty too. Select it, and every word on screen is the entry’s own name — this “translation table” sits in column 0 of texts.csv: 5,755 data rows, all 5,755 cells equal to the row name, written by the client itself.
The repo had only ever treated TID as “the name of column 0” and never used it. Now ?lang=TID is the 21st shipped language, and it’s in the language selector too. When writing tests I use it as a two-sided check: on the same page ZH-HANS is still “Build”, while on the TID page it should be TID_BUTTON_BUILD.
 The cost
For every column you add, you have to change the engine’s catalog, the JSON keys, the shell rendering, the allowlist, and at least four regression tests at the same time, then go to the build machine and run the entire remote_acceptance.sh. The entry allowlist grew from 26 to 86 items, the languages went from 20 to 21, and 422 of the 425 objects can be matched to client TIDs.
But what you get in exchange is a different kind of commit message: no longer “fix the values,” but “these four columns weren’t read before and are now; how should the regressions be re-run?” When the client updates, toss the new csv/ into the corpus and fix whatever goes red—the source of truth isn’t on my side; hand-copying is what needs justification.
(This is part 2 of 2 of the same post.)

title: After moving the secret key out of _config.yml, every command has to remember to include the other config file
content:
A string of commits on the morning of August 4 had one theme: clearing sensitive values out of the blog config — the Baidu/Bing push tokens, the api_key used for LLM tagging, the passphrase for encrypted post categories — all moved into _config.local.yml of .gitignore, leaving only a _config.local.example.yml template in the repo.
Three related things happened the same day: the comment system moved from Twikoo+Waline to Artalk, the license changed from CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 to CC BY 4.0, and AI crawlers were let through with llms.txt generated. This post is about the cost of config layering, plus the GEO and attribution side of things.
 De-sensitizing isn’t deleting the values
_config.yml is public, so writing a key into it is the same as publishing it. But a Hexo build still needs the real values, so the approach is layering:
# _config.local.example.yml（进仓库）
hexo_submit_urls_to_search_engine:
  baidu_token: ""
  bing_token: ""
llm_tagging:
  api_key: ""
encrypt:
  categories:
    - { name: 加密, password: "" }
Copy it to _config.local.yml and fill in the real values; the build deep-merges them with --config _config.yml,_config.local.yml. All four scripts — build / server / dev / push — have the merge arguments built in.
The upside is obvious: no real values in the repo, and the template tells the next person what to fill in. The downside is just as obvious: every command has to remember to carry that second config file, and forgetting it doesn’t throw an error — it degrades silently.
 The two directions of forgetting
The first direction is a build that fails outright. After api_key was moved out of llm_tagging, _config.yml is left with only an empty parent key, and running hexo clean without --config throws an error on the empty config. So the hexo clean in clean and dev got the merge arguments too — even a command like “clean”, which looks unrelated to config, has to carry them.
The second direction is subtler: leave out the passphrase for encrypt.categories and the build won’t fail — posts in encrypted categories are simply output in plaintext. So there’s a warning line next to the encrypt block in _config.yml:
# ⚠ 不带 _config.local.yml 合并构建时，加密分类的文章会以明文输出
A config whose failure mode is “leak” is far more dangerous than one whose failure mode is “error”. The former needs someone to actively go look; the latter at least goes red.
 The GEO part
Also that day: robots.txt now explicitly allows the major AI crawlers — GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, Google-Extended, CCBot and friends — and points at llms.txt and the two sitemaps; a new scripts/llms-txt.js was added, generating /llms.txt at build time.
The generator groups by first category, one - [标题](绝对URL): 摘要 line per post, and the summary strips code blocks, HTML and Markdown marks, truncated to 100 characters. Two edge cases are worth mentioning:

Encrypted posts are kept out of llms.txt so the summary can’t leak. After hexo-blog-encrypt processing, password is deleted from the post object, so the check has to re-read the frontmatter from the source file — the in-memory object can’t be trusted;
An individual post can opt out with llms: false in its front-matter.

On the sitemap side I tried hexo-generator-seo-friendly-sitemap's index-style splitting and rolled back to the official hexo-generator-sitemap two and a half minutes later: the site has only about 80 posts, so splitting into post/page/category/tag tables buys too little, and the official plugin is more actively maintained anyway. The llms.txt and robots changes stayed.
 Attribution and license
Also that day, seven AI-drafted posts uniformly got copyright_author: Claude Opus 4.8 and copyright_author_href added, so the “article author” in the copyright box shows the collaborator instead of just me.
The license moved from CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 to CC BY 4.0: attribution, commercial use and derivatives allowed. I thought one thing through while making the change — a fair amount of what’s on the blog was already assembled from client-side corpora, official docs and material from all over, and the friction of the non-commercial restriction outweighed the benefit.
 Wrapping up
After config layering, the public repo really is clean, but the system’s default state changed too: previously "just run hexo g" would build a correct site; now you have to remember the merge. Wiring it into every entry point only makes it the default, not automatic — anyone cloning the repo still has to cp the template and fill in values.
If someone asks again someday why the keys can’t just go back into _config.yml, the answer isn’t the word “insecure” — it’s: the public config and the buildable config are two different things from now on.

title: The Year-Rollover Trap of a Date Input: Read the Year Back Before Saving
content:
There’s a page on the site called /masturbation that publicly shows each day’s count and an annual heatmap, plus an admin backend /dash/masturbation where the administrator can backfill, edit, and clear entries. The data is private and the page is ordinary: a year-scoped query RPC, a calendar, a date input and a count input.
On launch day there was a bug that silently ate data.
 0 means both “nothing that day” and “zero out that day”
The heatmap loads by year, and the editor’s selectedCount comes from the current year’s query result. On the 2025 page, the admin changes the date to 2024-03-12—

The date in the input changes, but the page still holds 2025 data;
selectedCount can’t find that day in the 2025 array and falls back to 0;
The count input shows 0;
Click save, and 0 is written.

If 2024-03-12 originally had 7 recorded, that one “nothing was changed” save wipes it out. Here 0 is both the display default for “no record” and the write value for “clear the record” — the two look exactly alike.
 Let the date carry its own year
The first instinct might be to add a hint: “switch the year first for cross-year dates.” But the more reliable fix is to make the year part of the selection state:

Selecting a date that doesn’t belong to the current year immediately navigate('?year=2024&date=2024-03-12');
The loader loads that year’s data based on the year param, and brings the initial selected value back in via the date param;
The route component uses year:initialDate as the key, so the whole editor remounts when crossing years;
Until the new data arrives, the save button is disabled.

The key guard is this line:
const unavailable =
  busy || navigation.state !== 'idle' || Number(selected.slice(0, 4)) !== year
As long as the selected year differs from the current page’s year, saving isn’t allowed. That way, even if navigation is slow and the user is fast, the 0 from “last year hasn’t been read back yet” never gets written.
After a successful save, instead of refetching the whole year, update the local days with the returned value: if the count is greater than 0, replace or insert; if it’s 0, remove it from the array. The old useQuery + invalidateQueries are gone too, saving a round trip and removing the need to maintain the retry branch for when the query.isError refresh fails.
 The heatmap itself isn’t that mysterious
The calendar lays out cells using UTC dates: from January 1 of the year back to that week’s Sunday, then day by day forward past January 1 of the next year and filled out to a full week. The page has 365 or 366 buttons, future dates are disabled, and counts only take rows from <= today. Month labels compute the column number from which week the 1st of each month lands in; the annual total, days recorded, and single-day maximum are all derived from the counts.
today uses Intl.DateTimeFormat to pin Asia/Shanghai, so it doesn’t read the server process timezone. Both /masturbation and the admin send Cache-Control: no-store, so an anonymous user clicking save gets a 401.
Links between the public page and the admin, the previous year’s ←, and the next year’s → are all there; the year is only allowed from 1970 through the current year, illegal years get a 400 and no fake records are generated. The initial table is just empty — no sample data is stuffed in.
 Phone width
The same round also fixed overflow in the admin at 390×844: outer flex-wrap, date input min-w-0 max-w-full, stat cards changed from a fixed three columns to repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 100px), 1fr)), year heading whitespace-nowrap. The e2e asserts documentElement.scrollWidth <= innerWidth.
The heatmap itself allows horizontal scrolling on narrow screens, but only inside the chart — it doesn’t stretch the whole page.
 How to nail down the regression
The new e2e first saves 2024-03-12 as 7, then opens the 2025 admin, fills in this cross-year date, asserts that the count input becomes 7 within 1.5 seconds, clicks save, and finally checks the year endpoint that it’s still 7. In finally it writes the original value back, so other cases aren’t polluted.
The other case only does the phone-width check. Neither relies on “the user remembering to switch the year first.”
 Wrapping up
The implicit primary key of a time-series form is (year, day). Choosing across years isn’t changing a string — it’s switching the data source; treating “loading” as a disable condition is more reliable than any hint.
Fields like 0, which are both a value and a default, are most dangerous when they get submitted as the “current value” before the data has arrived. Read it back first, then allow writes.

title: Rate Limiting Before the Write: Debugging a Verification Code Invalidated by Itself
content:
In September’s auth milestone, email OTP, password reset, and Google login all wrapped up together. Among the things the first review round turned up, one was related to rate limiting, and I’m writing it down because it’s nothing like “just configuring a few numbers.”
 Look at the code order first
better-auth’s email-otp plugin first calls resolveOTP (email-otp/routes.mjs:31) in the endpoint, unconditionally inserting a code row; the sendVerificationOTP callback that sends the email only runs after that. On consumption, consumeVerificationValue (internal-adapter.mjs:818-860) only ever recognizes “the latest row for that identifier,” and on consumption it deleteMany all rows.
The old code hung the rate-limit check inside the send-email callback, i.e. after that insert. Once it tripped:

resolveOTP had already written a new code row;
The callback checked the rate limit, refused to send, and that row never reached anyone’s inbox;
The user entered the old code from the email in hand; it matched the latest row, and INVALID_OTP;
Both rows were wiped together.

The user was stuck: the code in their inbox was dead, no new code could be obtained within the cooldown window, and the error message said “invalid code,” putting the blame on the user.
 Move it before the insert
The fix is to block at hooks.before. The dispatch supports a before hook returning an object without the context key to short-circuit (the end of runBeforeHooks + else if (before) in dispatchAuthEndpoint), the endpoint handler doesn’t run at all, and that row never gets written.
All three invariants were kept, each with its own assertion:

The rate-limited response is byte-for-byte identical to the “email not registered” response (status code + body + content-type all compared);
Rate-limited requests send no email;
The first request in the window still sends exactly one email. With the check running before the insert, the old -1 compensation in assertOtpRateExcludingCurrent was deleted too.

 The rate-limit layer itself turns into a registration oracle
The second version’s problem was subtler. resolveOTP leaves a persistent verification row for a registered email, but better-auth immediately deletes the just-inserted row for an unregistered email (enumeration defense — both request-password-reset and forget-password/email-otp do this).
