If a rate-limit hit threw 429, then hammering the same address twice would directly tell an attacker whether that email has an account, depending on whether the status code sequence was (200,429) or (200,200).
Before the identifier format was fixed, the counter was mute — it neither protected nor leaked; after the fix, the counter actually started counting registered emails for the first time, and the side effect became observable.



Path
On rate-limit hit
Rationale




Password reset
Silently skip sending, endpoint still returns 200
“Rate-limited” and “email doesn’t exist” must be indistinguishable


Email verification
429
The sign-up endpoint already leaks the same fact once via USER_ALREADY_EXISTS_USE_ANOTHER_EMAIL, and /verify's resend button needs real feedback



One footnote to this table: whoever one day plugs the sign-up leak must at the same time change the email-verification 429 to a silent short-circuit, otherwise it’s only half plugged.
 Rejected requests must not leave a row
The hourly quota counts rows in the verification table. In the old implementation, rejected requests also left a row, so an attacker could fill a victim’s quota with five straight hits — only one email actually went out, but the person was locked out for an hour.
With the check moved before resolveOTP, rejections leave no row. There’s a dedicated regression case:
expect(await countOtpRows('forget-password', email)).toBe(1)
Reverting would count to 2. What the quota should count is “emails actually sent.”
 Rescuing a one-shot path
The same round also had the squatting arbitration. When Google login hits an unverified email, it deletes the squatter’s password in databaseHooks.account.create.after. The function had only been reasoned through for “a crash between the two deletes,” never for “any throw anywhere in the function body”:
create.after → queueAfterTransactionHook (with-hooks.mjs:33 didn’t give onError, re-throws as-is) → createWithHooks → linkAccount → generic catch, returns unable to link account. And the account row is already committed; a throw can’t undo it.
The user sees one login failure, retries → takes the already-linked branch (link-account.mjs 135–181); that branch doesn’t trigger the hook but does set emailVerified to true. Endgame: the email is verified, the victim logged in with Google, the squatter’s password still works as usual, and it’s indistinguishable in hindsight — it looks exactly like “an already-verified account hooked up to Google.”
The fix is to wrap the whole function body in try/catch, swallow it, don’t rethrow, and just log a single [auth] 抢注仲裁失败 … entry with the userId. The reason for not rethrowing is written in the comment: throwing can’t undo the already-committed link, it only adds one more inexplicable login failure, and the retry takes the branch that doesn’t even log, which buries the hole deeper. The test mocks db.transaction to make it throw, asserting the return is false, the log has the userId, and the password is still there.
 “Please verify your email first” needs to actually be clickable
Someone else in the same round hit another one: they registered, closed the tab, came back the next day to post, and got stopped by a 403 saying “Please verify your email before posting content.” — a dead end with nothing clickable in it, and site-wide /verify only links out from the registration page and the Google button. Even if you found /verify, the page opens by announcing “a verification code has been sent to your email,” but that page never sends a code on load — the line is a lie.
We changed email_unverified to render as "copy + a link to /verify", across eight user-side render points. The copy in /verify became “Enter the 6-digit code you received… if it didn’t arrive, hit the button below to request one”, updated in all three languages; the resend button moved from ghost to outline. No auto-send on page entry — that would burn the per-email hourly quota on every refresh.
 An Empty String Is Not “Not Configured”
There’s another of the same kind on the deployment side. The docs say in four places that “omitting the email variables doesn’t error, it just behaves wrong; if MAIL_TRANSPORT isn’t passed it defaults to console.” That’s false: Compose substitutes host variables that were never set with an empty string, and ?? 'console' and .default() only accept undefined; parseMailEnv({ MAIL_TRANSPORT: '' }) throws outright, and the symptom is that the api container won’t start.
Crashing is the better behavior, so we didn’t grant empty strings an exemption — instead we wrote the contract down clearly: this group of variables must exist and be non-empty, and if the container won’t start, check the email config first. Two assertions in mail/config.test.ts pin it down.
The test and e2e scripts, meanwhile, hard-prefix MAIL_TRANSPORT=console. Shell environment variables take precedence over --env-file, so without that prefix, once you’ve set MAIL_TRANSPORT to resend locally: a single test run fires off a batch of real emails to actual inboxes, and e2e fails outright because it can’t read the verification code from stdout.
 Wrapping Up
Rate limiting isn’t a set of numbers, it’s a position in the write order. Get the position wrong and what it stops isn’t the attacker — it’s the email in the user’s hands.
Later, all of these became assertions: the bytes of a 429, only one email sent, no row left behind on rejection, userId preserved on failure, empty string must crash. Individually they look trivial, but only together do they show that rate limiting ended up in the right place.

title: What I'm Doing When Eight Tracks Run in Parallel
content:
Before writing this, I glanced at the build machine: 5 tmux sessions running, 372 task directories under ~/.local/state/ai-jobs totaling 3.1 GB, load average 2.90 and drifting between two and seven the whole time. The machine has 128 cores, up for four and a half days. Those numbers are a single sampled instant—they’d changed again by the time I finished this paragraph, which is itself part of the point.
The projects on hand at the same moment: a Rust + SQL site reworking its statistics query, a Next.js app retiring its service worker, a Bun + Hono service fixing a tunnel origin, a Prisma + tRPC monorepo, a C# game private server filling in data fields, a C/C++ SDL3/WASM port, and two Zola/Hexo documentation sites. 64 directories and 36 git repositories under ~/Code.
This isn’t the “I have a lot of windows open” kind of parallelism. Anyone can open windows; the hard part is making progress on all of them at once without contaminating each other.
 First, why it’s even worth it
With a single project, the most expensive part of AI collaboration is waiting: ten minutes for a full test run, five for a build, however long for browser regression. During that time the only things a person can do are sit there or switch to something else—and switching back means reloading context.
The first payoff of running eight projects in parallel is exactly this: the waiting gets filled by other lines. A’s build is running while B’s failure log just comes back; C waits on a human confirmation while D’s tests go red and need fixing. The machine’s throughput gets pulled up, and the human brain no longer has idle gaps.
The second payoff is reusing a solution from one line on another. Today, figuring out in av-site that “creating an index must stay inside the same transaction block as acquiring the lock” naturally led to thinking about “the deletion order when retiring a worker” in AstroDX—both are cases of “nothing can slip in between the two steps.” That kind of cross-project intuition only happens when you have several lines in hand at once.
But the payoff has preconditions, and here they are.
 Rules must be layered, not copied
~/.agents/AGENTS.md is the single source of truth; ~/.codex/AGENTS.md and ~/.dsh/AGENTS.md are symlinks to it, and ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md references it via @. To change a rule you only change that one copy—three copies will inevitably drift.
The source of truth holds only what’s universal across projects: hold conversations in Chinese, Conventional Commits, the local machine isn’t the build machine, which machine to go to remotely, how to persist tasks over 30 seconds, where the proxy is.
Project-level AGENTS.md files only describe what’s unique to that project, and some really do write them narrowly:

av-site/AGENTS.md: all five CI steps green is the prerequisite for merging; changing OpenAPI types requires bun run gen:client; how to spin up a temporary postgres for database tests with #[ignore]; curl from the build machine needs a UA or Cloudflare returns 403; add SET default_transaction_read_only = on; before production troubleshooting.
eagler-touhou-next/AGENTS.md: this Mac is read/write and Git only; which checkout directory on the build machine; bun is pinned to 1.4.2; where the project’s own postgres:18 container lives.
th15/AGENTS.md is only 15 lines: the ownership of two trees.

That middle category—“which machine is the build machine”—is actually written in both files. It looks redundant, but the division of labor differs: the source of truth says “there is a build machine, pick by priority,” while the project file says “this project is fixed to this one, the checkout directory is here.” The former is a rule, the latter a fact.
There’s one more hard rule: every project must be able to state clearly “where it runs”—if you can’t write it down, the project isn’t ready to be parallelized yet.
 Tasks must have an identity
Something run remotely can’t just be a ssh host 'bun run build' and done with it—drop the SSH and it’s gone, and reconnecting doesn’t tell you where it got to.
The rule in the source of truth, “remote SSH task persistence and reconnection recovery,” specifies this (shared by all projects):
Each task gets an independent ID, an independent tmux session, and an independent ~/.local/state/ai-jobs/<任务ID>/ directory. Inside the directory, run.sh begins with set -uo pipefail, umask 077, exec > output.log, trap writing the exit code into a file, echo $$ > pid, date -Is > started, then explicitly exporting PATH and HTTP(S)_PROXY.
Startup, logs, exit code, process ID, and start time are all five on disk. If SSH drops, go back by the original ID and read the status—do not resubmit. If the tmux session is gone but there’s also no exit code, the status counts as unknown: keep cross-checking the process and artifacts, and don’t treat it as success or as failure.
What’s forbidden is sharing a fixed ai-task session—several lines firing send-keys into the same session amounts to throwing commands into a shell you don’t recognize.
Recent tasks’ exit codes include both 0 and 1 (adjust-download-policy-red is 1, adjust-prod-cold is 1, a batch of adjust-consent mixed 1/0). Parallelism isn’t eight lines all green—it’s eight lines’ results each landing on disk, each queryable, with the red ones not dragging the others down.
 Write to one place at a time
Two lines editing the same file at once is the number-one incident source in this workflow.
The unit of dispatch isn’t the project, it’s the file. Today the write-sets of the four lines are: av-site/infra/migrations/*, AstroDX/apps/web/public + src/lib, acgn-flow/src/server/*, drama-site/apps/web/src/*. The four groups are mutually disjoint.
(This is part 1 of 2 of the same post.)
Conversely, if the same package.json or root tsconfig needs to be changed, make them sequentially dependent: finish one before starting the next. Hard parallelism here only produces git conflicts and edits that overwrite each other.
When shared configuration must be changed across projects, I’d rather pause the line I’m on and wait for it to land.
 Verification is tiered by scope of change
What most easily slackens under parallelism is verification, because every line wants to wrap up quickly.
The rule is tier by change, not by how much time is free:

One file changed → lint just that file, run just that test file; it can be done locally.
Cross-module change → go up to the build machine and run the whole-repo check for that project (AstroDX’s scripts/remote/verify.sh runs 739 tests + lints 719 files).
Anything with side effects (migrations, deployments, data fixes) → add real-device acceptance; for example, av-site changes to playback must run check-live-playback.py with a rate-limit round, and all-green smoke isn’t enough.

The only valid reason to downgrade verification is “this change isn’t worth that cost,” never “I’m busy right now.” Being busy is precisely what parallelism creates; trading busyness for cheap verification just pays back the time parallelism saved.
 The costs, recorded in plain sight
The above is method; below is the ledger.
Context dilutes itself. With eight lines in hand, the memory of each grows thin. So the moment a line lands, “why it was changed this way” must go straight into a code comment or that project’s docs—don’t count on remembering next time. Of the 86 lines in 0055's migration file, 52 are comments, and AstroDX’s docs/verification/service-worker-retirement-2026-10-30.md even records when the script itself went wrong—both for this reason.
Review is the bottleneck, and it doesn’t scale with parallelism. Eight lines each produce output, and the merge decision all lands on one person. So better to let the AI go slower and produce less than to have it change 20 files at once—a giant change that can’t be decomposed takes longer to read through than to do yourself.
Build-machine resources are shared. A load average of two to seven looks low, but that’s headroom on 128 cores; at the same moment, two or three of several tmux sessions are running browser regressions and competing for memory. Lines running full test suites need to be scheduled on idle cores; single-core cases like taskset -c 0 get slowed by other lines, and timing issues on a slow CPU only surface under that condition—which is both a blessing and a trap.
Task directories grow if not cleaned. 372 directories, 3.1 GB, four and a half days of uptime. After a run, --keep keeps the evidence, and it should be swept a week later; it hasn’t been swept yet, which already counts as debt.
One more thing often overlooked: parallelism makes “done” cheap. One line goes red and nobody cares; another goes green and keeps moving, and the red one gets buried. So at the end of each day, look through the directories with non-zero exit codes, not at “how many were delivered today.”
 Who this suits
Who it doesn’t suit: people whose changes are strongly linear, who can only think about one thing at a time, who dislike writing rule files.
There’s only one prerequisite for it to suit you: the project must already be verifiable in a remote form. A build machine, a verify script, and “where to run it” written into files—with all three in place you can split lines; missing any one, and raising parallelism only moves “stuck” from local to remote.
As for the AI’s side, it neither knows nor cares that other lines are running. It’s kept apart by the “don’t touch that directory” constraints in rule files, by the identity of task directories, by disjoint write sets. All these partitions are built in advance by a human; the AI just runs inside them.
When eight lines run at once, what I’m actually doing is quite boring: reading exit codes, watching logs, judging which line should continue and which should stop, writing the reasons into files. The real parallelism happens on disk and CPU; the human part remains serial—except what’s serialized is judgment, not typing.
(This is part 2 of 2 of the same post.)

title: After Pulling EXISTS Out of the FILTER
content:
The detail page for channel stats takes 1.5 seconds. On a backend dashboard that’s not a disaster, but waiting a second and a half on every refresh is something users remember.
The baseline is a production scale of 246,000 clicks over a 30-day window. The detail page takes 1.51 s, the cross-channel overview 1.49 s, and the share page 0.85 s—the share page is shown to advertisers, and a second and a half of white screen looks bad.
 The problem isn’t data volume
First, let’s clarify the term “valid device”: among distinct devices, those that actually landed within 30 minutes of the click. The criterion is a macro called LANDED, whose core is a single EXISTS, querying a idx_channel_pv_device built on 0067 (keyed by device + timestamp).
The original approach stuffed LANDED inside an aggregate FILTER:
count(DISTINCT c.device_id) FILTER (WHERE NOT c.is_bot AND {LANDED}) AS valid_devices
It looks natural enough—that’s exactly what FILTER is for. But EXISTS here is a correlated subquery, and the planner generates a SubPlan for it—meaning it runs once per real click. Over a 30-day window that’s 230,000 index probes, and this item alone accounts for 680 milliseconds.
The fix was to extract the whole “valid devices” concept into a standalone subquery, with LANDED written into its WHERE:
(SELECT count(DISTINCT c.device_id) FROM channel_click c
  WHERE c.channel_code = $1 AND c.clicked_at >= $2 AND c.clicked_at < $3
    AND NOT c.is_bot AND {LANDED})
Now the planner can see it: this is a semi-join between the click table and the landing table, hashable in one pass instead of 230,000 probes. That part goes from 680 ms → 300 ms.
The daily trend and per-channel list follow the same logic, rewritten as a single grouped subquery with LEFT JOIN. The caller of with_valid = false (the share page doesn’t show valid devices) saves even more—the subquery disappears entirely, replaced by a constant 0, without scanning the click table again.
 But half the time is still there
After the semi-join rewrite, a large chunk of the remaining time is compilation overhead.
These SQL statements are sub-second OLTP queries; JIT is never worthwhile, yet the planner keeps triggering it by mistake. The reason is that the daily query uses generate_series left joins, and the row estimate comes out to about 200 million, far above the jit_above_cost threshold. A single JIT compilation takes 150–550 milliseconds, eating more than half of an already sub-second query.
So I added a read-only transaction to the stats endpoint:
async fn stats_tx(pool: &sqlx::PgPool) -> Result<sqlx::Transaction<'_, sqlx::Postgres>, AppError> {
    let mut tx = pool.begin().await?;
    sqlx::Executor::execute(
        &mut *tx,
        "SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY; SET LOCAL jit = off; SET LOCAL plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan",
    ).await?;
    Ok(tx)
}
Three details:

A parameterless &str uses the simple query protocol, so all three statements go in one round trip.
I didn’t use sqlx::raw_sql—its execute would make the caller’s (the axum handler’s) future fail the Send check.
SET LOCAL only applies to this transaction and reverts once the connection returns to the pool; the transaction is read-only, so dropping (rolling back) at the end is enough.

 The third directive was the most surprising
I didn’t initially think to add plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan.
Here’s the thing: sqlx caches prepared statements on the connection. After the same statement runs 5 times, Postgres switches to a generic plan—because a generic plan saves the 1–3 ms of replanning each time, a win for most high-frequency short queries.
But a generic plan can’t see the actual parameter values, hence not the window boundaries, so it estimates the time range as tiny. With the window estimated too small, the hash semi-join I’d just built degrades into a row-by-row nested loop. The funnel goes from 290 ms → 600 ms, twice as slow as before the fix, and it only starts being slow on the 6th request.
This isn’t visible to the naked eye. I wrote a throwaway test that ran the same batch of handler functions eight times in a row on the same connection to see the curve.
These endpoints aren’t hit often anyway, so an extra 1–3 ms of planning per call is negligible. So I forced a custom plan, always taking the measured hash semi-join.
 How I proved the results didn’t change
Performance changes are the easiest way to accidentally alter semantics. This time I required byte-for-byte consistency, verifying two things:

The funnel row: compare md5 directly.
The md5 of the daily rows and the per-channel rows.

I verified both the 30-day and 7-day windows. Only when everything matched did I accept it.
Results (30-day window, benchmarked on the build machine):



Endpoint
Before
After




Channel detail
1.51 s
0.64 s


Cross-channel overview
1.49 s
0.72 s


Share page
0.85 s
0.55 s



 A few takeaways
A correlated subquery inside FILTER becomes a per-row SubPlan. As long as it can be extracted wholesale, extracting it is almost always the right call; FILTER is fine for cheap scalar checks, not for EXISTS.
"It’s faster after the change" isn’t necessarily true. This time, if I’d only looked at the first-run benchmark and not the curve after the 6th run, the conclusion would have been exactly the opposite. Slow queries in production often only show up after a connection has been reused for a while; a single benchmark won’t catch it.
JIT isn’t only enabled for big queries. It’s triggered by the estimated row count, and estimates can easily be pushed above the threshold by things like generate_series. Sub-second queries should just turn it off explicitly.
On top of stats_tx there’s also a coverage test: use a single-connection pool (only then is the connection fetched after the transaction ends guaranteed to be the same one, which is how you can tell whether SET LOCAL leaked into the pool), assert that all three settings really took effect inside the transaction, then try inserting a row in there and assert that it fails, and finally drop the transaction and re-run SHOW on the pool for jit and plan_cache_mode, which must be back to the default on / auto. If SET LOCAL leaks into the pool it contaminates every later query, which is far worse than being a bit slow.
These lessons now live in the function comments, right next to the code. If I’d written them in a blog post, three months later I wouldn’t be able to find them myself…

title: That One Comment Earned at the Cost of Production Downtime
content:
In the opening comment of infra/migrations/0055_work_code_case_uniq.sql there’s a passage that was bought with a real production outage. Before I wrote it, I first wrote down a judgment — and production shot that judgment down…
Let me lay out the background first, otherwise that comment just reads like generic hand-wringing.
 What we’re fixing isn’t “can’t find it”
0001_init.sql hands work.code a bare TEXT UNIQUE, i.e. UNIQUE (code), case-sensitive. But every read path on the site matches on lower(code) = lower($1).
The consequence of that mismatch isn’t “can’t find it” — it’s one title splitting into two rows in the database. In the 2026-08 batch the catalog pusher started sending the code as DASS-966 instead of dass-966; upsert_work's ON CONFLICT (code) didn’t match, so a new row got inserted. In production, three pairs actually split: DASS-966, DSOD-009, START-597 — merged by hand on 2026-08-29.
The symptoms after a split aren’t errors either; they’re two classes of silent failure:

Half the data. The old row holds source_link, work_embedding, frame_embedding; the new row has only metadata. And ... WHERE lower(w.code)=lower($1) LIMIT 1 has no ORDER BY, so which row you get is up to the query plan. At the time, DSOD-009 and START-597 were getting the row with no play sources — the watch page returned 200 with not a single source.
A flat 500. Any scalar subquery of the shape = (SELECT ... WHERE lower(code)=lower($1)) raises more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression when it hits multiple rows. Unfavorite, remove-from-playlist, and the similar-titles fallback all have that shape.

At the time, 0046_anime_import.sql:117-131 deliberately didn’t create the unique index right away, on the grounds that the existing dirty data would blow up the entire --single-transaction migration. Now that the data is merged clean, 0055 is here to tighten things up.
 Why keep that case-sensitive constraint
What we’re creating is CREATE UNIQUE INDEX work_code_lower_key ON work (lower(code)). So can the old work_code_key (UNIQUE (code)) just be dropped along the way?
No. external_source_map.code is a foreign key pointing at work(code), and a foreign key requires a unique constraint on the referenced column, so DROP work_code_key would fail on dependency. And UNIQUE (lower(code)) is strictly stronger than it, so keeping it has no downside.
The non-unique functional index idx_work_lower_code created by 0046 can go, though — same columns, fully covered by the new unique index; keeping it just adds write amplification.
 First judgment call: why it’s all wrapped in one DO block
Because LOCK TABLE only works inside a transaction block.
The production migration goes through psql --single-transaction in migrate.sh, which has a transaction block — no problem. But the local procedure recorded in tools/ugc-smoke/README.md is per-file psql -f, autocommit, no transaction block — a bare LOCK there just errors with LOCK TABLE can only be used in transaction blocks, and the local smoke DB ends up missing this unique constraint, which is the one and only thing this migration does.
A DO block carries its own implicit transaction, so it holds under both procedures. That also explains why LOCK and CREATE INDEX can’t be split into two statements.
 Why grab the strongest lock right at the start
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX takes a SHARE lock, which blocks writes; DROP INDEX needs ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. Create-then-drop means a second lock upgrade inside the same transaction.
An online write that squeezes in between (the UPDATE work in increment_view) can’t get RowExclusive and queues; we then wait for it to yield; a cycle forms; deadlock detected; the whole migration rolls back. This was reproduced on the production database.
There’s an easy assumption to make: “nobody’s writing while the migration runs anyway.” It doesn’t hold: compose runs migrate to completion before it touches the api container, so during the migration the old api is still serving and increment_view keeps writing.
So one LOCK TABLE work IN ACCESS EXCLUSIVE MODE at the top grabs the strongest lock and never upgrades again — a cycle has no way to form.
 Second judgment call: this is where I got it wrong
The first time this went to prd, lock_timeout was followed by “fail fast if the lock can’t be had.” The reasoning at the time: migrate exits non-zero, the api isn’t rebuilt, the old api keeps serving — so failing is the safe direction.
That judgment was wrong.
docker compose up -d does not preserve the old container just because migrate exited non-zero. It rebuilds api/web as usual; the new container just gets stuck at Created and won’t come up — depends_on: migrate: service_completed_successfully isn’t satisfied.
Net result: the migration didn’t take effect and the site went down outright. And the prd work table always has increment_view writing to it, so there was never any guarantee of grabbing ACCESS EXCLUSIVE within 15 seconds. An ordinary deploy took the site out.
The right approach is short timeout + repeated retries: wait only 2 seconds each round, let the queued write transactions finish, then try again. Online writes are all short transactions, so within a few rounds a window is bound to open. Only if 60 seconds pass without getting the lock do we RAISE — that means a long transaction is sitting on work, which calls for human intervention rather than forcing it.
FOR i IN 1..30 LOOP
    BEGIN
        PERFORM set_config('lock_timeout', '2s', true);
        LOCK TABLE work IN ACCESS EXCLUSIVE MODE;
        EXIT;
    EXCEPTION WHEN lock_not_available THEN
        IF i = 30 THEN
            RAISE EXCEPTION '60 秒内拿不到 work 的 ACCESS EXCLUSIVE 锁（有长事务压着？先查 pg_stat_activity 再重试）';
        END IF;
        PERFORM pg_sleep(1);
    END;
END LOOP;
PERFORM set_config('lock_timeout', '0', true);
A separate BEGIN/EXCEPTION per round creates an implicit savepoint, so a failed lock attempt rolls back only that round and doesn’t poison the whole migration transaction.
 Error messages need to speak human
There’s one more gate before you create the unique index. If duplicates exist, it hands back a sentence you can act on directly, rather than a duplicate key value:
SELECT count(*), string_agg(lc, ', ' ORDER BY lc)
  INTO dup, sample
  FROM (SELECT lower(code) AS lc FROM work GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) > 1 LIMIT 20) t;
IF dup > 0 THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION
      'work 存在 % 组大小写重复 code，须先人工合并（保留握有 source_link/向量的那行）再跑本迁移：%',
      dup, sample;
END IF;
“Keep the row that holds the source_link” has to be written in — reverse the merge direction and data is still lost, the unique index still gets built, and from then on that movie simply has no playback source.
 Wrapping Up
EXECUTE 'DROP INDEX IF EXISTS idx_work_lower_code';
EXECUTE 'CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS work_code_lower_key ON work (lower(code))';
Both go through EXECUTE: inside a DO block you could write the DDL directly, but the whole script uniformly uses EXECUTE to concatenate strings, tied together with the variables above so it reads as one thing from start to finish.
At the end of the migration file there’s also a ANALYZE work;, so the planner sees the new index as quickly as possible.
Looking back now, the file is 86 lines in total, and comments account for 52 of them. The longest passage is the record of that outage, reading “⚠️ This one was bought with production downtime”… Without it written down, the next person (or me three months later) will see “2 seconds × 30” and just think it’s verbose, then optimize it back to “fail fast.”

title: The Typecheck Was Green After the Merge
content:
2aa1194ed, titled “Merge latest main into zsf”. A completely ordinary merge commit.
It deleted the entire Adjust runtime. Under packages/api/src/adjust/, 7 of the 8 files were deleted outright, and diff --stat was 4 insertions and 292 deletions.
No conflicts. No compile errors. CI was green.
 How the deletion slipped in
The merge’s two parents are e5051db93 and 93173a00b (main), and the merge base is e11e286ff. On the base, these 8 files were intact, and all the git ls-tree references were present.
The problem was that the zsf line had already deleted them: that line was meant to implement a different feature, and from its perspective Adjust was “something extra that existed on main,” so removing it made the local tree cleaner. When merging, git therefore faced “deleted on one side, untouched on the other”—under the three-way merge rules, the deletion counts as zsf’s change and is kept as-is.
This is not a revert, nor is it a conflict. A conflict at least stops and asks you. This kind of merge takes effect silently, and the commit message only says “Merge latest main.”
Even more conveniently, there were no compile errors after the deletion. That’s because in the same batch of commits, all references to import "@nq/api/adjust", adjust-tracking, and adjust-session were deleted along with it—otherwise, with the references still present and the implementation gone, pnpm typecheck would have gone red.
So the whole set of green lights—“tests green, typecheck green, build green”—was completely useless here. They check whether it compiles, not whether the feature is still there.
 How it was found
A single command:
git grep '@nq/api/adjust' upstream/preview
Zero hits.
That was the lesson, short enough to serve as a mantra: After merging across major branches, don’t just look at typecheck—grep for the feature name. If a few more people merge after 2aa1194ed, this clue will be completely buried—the feature name is still in the docs, but the window in the minds of people who remember it is only a few days.
After it was found, 88cdad163 restored the runtime with 86 files and 6,117 insertions, filling in A2/A3/A4/A6/A7 all at once. As of 10-23, the audit document 09-adjust-audit.md still concluded “0%—there is no Adjust integration anywhere in the repository.”
Restoring it was only half the battle; the next part was where the real thinking began.
 8 Event Tokens are not 8 events
The vendor provided 8 Event Tokens, operations had already created them in the dashboard, and they required first purchase and refunds to carry amounts. The easiest implementation would be “send whenever you see a Token”—8 if statements.
But events are not equal. Split by “who is the single source of truth,” they fall into two categories from the start:



Event
Lane
Revenue




registration
SDK (native)
No


first_purchase
S2S
Yes


purchase
S2S
Yes


refund
S2S
Yes (refund amount)


first_unlock
S2S
No


episode_unlock
S2S
No


vip_activation
S2S
No


vip_expired
S2S
No



So the first thing the enqueueing code does is split the sets:
/** 带收入的事件 —— 入队时必须拿到合法金额与币种，否则落 BLOCKED 而不是发一条 0 元收入。 */
export const ADJUST_REVENUE_EVENTS: ReadonlySet<string> = new Set(
  ADJUST_INTERNAL_EVENTS.filter(e => e.revenue).map(e => e.key),
);
After the split, there are several rules hardcoded in the code and impossible to change from the dashboard.
One payment can only be recorded once. When first purchase matches, send only first_purchase and no longer send purchase:
function mappingCandidates(internalEvent: string, firstPurchase: boolean): string[] {
  if (!ADJUST_REVENUE_EVENTS.has(internalEvent)) return [internalEvent];
  const chain = internalEvent === "PURCHASE" || internalEvent === "FIRST_PURCHASE"
    ? ["PURCHASE"]
    : [internalEvent, "PURCHASE"];
  return firstPurchase ? ["FIRST_PURCHASE", ...chain] : chain;
}
The candidate order puts specific events before generic ones, and stops at the first match. When FIRST_PURCHASE is not configured, it naturally falls back to the type event or PURCHASE, and the whole chain doesn’t break just because one line is missing in the dashboard.
Non-revenue events have no fallback. Note that the first line above directly returns [internalEvent]. If EPISODE_UNLOCK lacks a mapping, it falls to BLOCKED / MISSING_S2S_MAPPING and does not fall back to PURCHASE—if it did, it would pointlessly record a 0-yuan revenue entry, creating a bunch of gaps in reports that are harder to trace than a missing entry.
Unlocks do not double-count revenue. Coins are bought in advance on top-up orders; unlocking merely spends them. Therefore, the revenue for first_unlock / episode_unlock is always empty.
Membership activation and revenue are two events from the same order. Both vip_activation and purchase are generated by the same order, so the unique key of the delivery row is expanded from (order_id, environment) to (order_id, environment, internal_event). currency is also made nullable at the same time—stuffing the string "INVALID" into non-revenue events would get rejected by the vendor’s currency validation.
Every missing piece must be visible. If any link in the chain is unsatisfied—no identity, environment mismatch, missing mapping, missing S2S token, invalid amount—write a BLOCKED row with a reason code; do not silently drop it. Black holes like “configured but no identity” must be visible in the dashboard’s postback records; otherwise you’ll forever be saying, “It should have been sent.”
 The callback side
GET|POST /api/webhooks/adjust/callback. Map status codes to their retry rules: 200 accepted or already received, 400 this one’s dead, don’t resend, 401 auth failed, 404 not paired yet, 503 our side had a temporary failure.
Auth nonce on both sides timingSafeEqual; the idempotency key is a hash of created_at; the receipt is pinned only on the first attempt (where callbackAt: null).
Once this was running, I ran into two vendor behaviors, both of which made it into code comments and tests:

2xx comes in three shapes: {"status":"OK"}, an empty body {}, and an empty string. The original check only recognized the first, so the other two were treated as UNKNOWN, and UNKNOWN doesn’t retry automatically — a payment already recorded on the vendor side would never reconcile. Changed it so any 2xx counts as SENT.
{order_id} is not a placeholder. It isn’t in the 262-entry placeholder table behind help.adjust.com, so writing it into the callback URL leaves it unreplaced and the other side receives the literal text. But the S2S callback_params appends the real value to the end of the URL, so the same key shows up twice, literal first, and first() always picks up {order_id}. The parser now walks getAll and skips {...}-shaped segments.

After the second fix I deliberately re-verified the worst case: reverted the template to the old form with {order_id}, created a transaction and ran it end to end, and the receipt got pinned as usual. Only after confirming that production was running the new parser — and not just “the template happened to be clean” — did I feel safe shipping it.
 Two gates, deliberately different
AD_REAL_SENDING_ENABLED=0 guards Meta CAPI and TikTok — neither has a sandbox, so a preview sends something that’s really recorded in the ad account. Adjust is therefore unaffected: it has a real sandbox, and adjustEnvironment() maps previews to SANDBOX.
To silence Adjust previews too, use the other gate, ADJUST_S2S_ENABLED=0.
The gates are separate because the reasons differ. One is “don’t pollute the real account”; the other is “this pipeline shuts itself up.” Merge them into one, and later, when you only want to silence one side, you’ll have to rewrite it.
 Wrapping up
Production is a separate a2bcb4351, based on release-v1.2.45, containing only what was verified on preview — no Mock/Kafka scaffolding and no consent modal.
In hindsight, the cost of a merge accident like 2aa1194ed isn’t in “getting it back” — from the merge (10-27 10:41 UTC+7) to the recovery commit 88cdad163 (same day, 19:47 UTC+8) was eight hours, and not a single line was lost from git. The cost is in those eight hours: the feature was assumed to “already exist,” nobody touched it, and regression tests can’t cover a module that doesn’t exist.
The cheapest line of defense is turning grep into a fixed post-merge step. Typecheck answers “does it compile”; only grep answers “is it still there.”

title: The server behind the tunnel thinks it's in HTTP
content:
The site is written in Bun + Hono, runs in a container, and is exposed via Cloudflare Tunnel. Five days ago there were two bugs in a row (be15f5a, 2ea4f53, eight minutes apart), both of which “brought local development assumptions into this topology.”
 First: origin is http
When the tunnel sends requests in from the public internet, the hop to the container is http. So anywhere that gets the origin via request.url gets http://....
Most places don’t care; two do:

the cookie’s Secure attribute, and OAuth callback URL construction—the callback comes out as http, but the browser treats the return as https, so they don’t match.
generating absolute URLs for external use (share links, links in emails)—what goes out is http, and when users click it they either get redirected or it simply doesn’t work.

Cloudflare includes x-forwarded-host and x-forwarded-proto. So should we restore based on those?
No. x-forwarded-host is a header the client can forge, and when connecting directly to the container port, it’s entirely determined by the requester. Trusting it unconditionally opens another hole for changing the origin.
I wrote a publicRequest(request, configuredUrl) (src/server/public-request.ts, 10 lines total), with these rules:

If no public domain is configured, return it as-is.
If the request host doesn’t match the configured host → leave it alone. That means it came in through another entry point (loopback preview, direct intranet connection), and that origin belongs to the user; changing it would actually be wrong.
If the hosts match but the protocol is already the same → leave it alone. Don’t copy the request for no reason.
The only remaining case: hosts match, protocols differ → change only the protocol and rebuild it with new Request().

const configured = new URL(configuredUrl);
const incoming = new URL(request.url);
if (incoming.host !== configured.host || incoming.protocol === configured.protocol)
  return request;
incoming.protocol = configured.protocol;
return new Request(incoming, request);
new Request(url, request) preserves the method, body, headers, and all other properties, replacing only the origin. In src/server/index.ts, change fetch: app.fetch to go through this handling before forwarding:
fetch: (...[request, bindings, executionCtx]: Parameters<typeof app.fetch>) =>
  app.fetch(publicRequest(request, process.env.APP_URL), bindings, executionCtx),
This way, “restoring https” only happens when it’s confirmed to be this entry point, and a forged x-forwarded-host is ignored because the host doesn’t match.
The three tests/public-request.test.ts cases cover exactly this: restoring https while keeping the POST body / cookies / query string all intact; not trusting x-forwarded-host: af.saop.cc when the actual connection is 127.0.0.1:31270; and returning the same object (rather than a copy) when the protocol is the same or no public domain is configured.
Strictly speaking, the third isn’t a security requirement but predictability—if you’re debugging locally with curl 127.0.0.1:3000 and suddenly see an https-style origin, you’d be suspicious for a long time.
 Second: the container’s 127.0.0.1 is not the host’s
For the container to access the internet, it has to go through the proxy 127.0.0.1:11090 on the host machine.
In compose.yaml it’s written like this:
environment:
  HTTP_PROXY: ${OUTBOUND_PROXY:-}
  HTTPS_PROXY: ${OUTBOUND_PROXY:-}
  NO_PROXY: ${OUTBOUND_NO_PROXY:-}
  http_proxy: ${OUTBOUND_PROXY:-}
  https_proxy: ${OUTBOUND_PROXY:-}
  no_proxy: ${OUTBOUND_NO_PROXY:-}
Both cases are written because Bun/undici recognizes lowercase, while many shell tools only recognize uppercase.
One pitfall has to be stated clearly right in .env.production.example:
# 宿主机上的代理，不是容器自己的 127.0.0.1
OUTBOUND_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:11090
OUTBOUND_NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1,postgres,redis
OUTBOUND_PROXY is set to 127.0.0.1, which points to the host’s loopback. But 127.0.0.1 inside the container is the container itself; if it doesn’t match, nothing on the network works. At the same time, NO_PROXY must include service names like postgres and redis—they’re on the same compose network, so connecting directly is faster than going through the proxy, and it also prevents the proxy from not recognizing those names.
 Don’t bake it into the image
The proxy is environment-specific: it exists on the build machine, may not exist on a laptop, and may use a different port in production. So inject it only at runtime via environment, and don’t write a single ENV HTTP_PROXY in Dockerfile.
If you bake it into the image, the image is tied to the network configuration at build time. Moreover, ENV in Dockerfile overrides runtime injection—you’d have to rebuild the image to change it, even though it’s clearly a configuration issue.
 What the two have in common
Both bugs have the same shape: the code was written assuming “requests connect directly, network connects directly,” but the deployment topology isn’t like that.
The tunnel and the container each work fine on their own; what’s missing is a layer of translation at their boundary—one translates the inbound origin from http back to https (and only when it should), and the other translates the outbound target from the container loopback to the host loopback.
Things at this kind of boundary have a characteristic: everything works locally, because locally it is both the “public entry point” and the “host machine,” so both assumptions hold at once. It only blows up after deployment, and the blow-up happens far from the change.
deploy/README.md now has explanations for both sections, placed together. Next time someone adds a new environment variable, they’ll at least see the sentence “the container and the host are two different loopbacks.”

title: Letting Service Worker Step Down on Its Own
